- verify(musl): static `nanocode` for x86_64-unknown-linux-musl and aarch64-unknown-linux-musl builds from master with no source change and passes the CLI smokes, natively and under qemu-aarch64 (2026-11-14, targets track). Built: `cargo build --locked -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` (static-pie) and `--target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` linked with clang `--target=aarch64-linux-musl -fuse-ld=lld` against Rust's self-contained musl (static). Run: output/tgt-smoke/smoke.sh, 11 of 11 on each: `--version`, `--help`, `psh-shell -c` exit status, pipes, arithmetic, file writes, globs, an external program and command substitution, and `nanocode exec` against a local mock of the Anthropic Messages API whose reply calls Code Mode `exec` with `tools.Bash`, which spawns `echo smoke-$((6*7))` and returns `smoke-42`, exit 0; the aarch64 binary under qemu-aarch64-static 8.2.2 registered with binfmt_misc so its re-exec as psh runs. Why: musl is what Pyramid's Hand ships, and the earlier musl runs (the libc-sys harness entries below) covered nanocode-sys's declarations, not the CLI.
- feat(riscv64): nanocode-sys declares the C library for riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu, every workspace crate but graviola and the crates that reach it builds there, and `nanocode-python` built for riscv64 runs under qemu-riscv64 with output identical to x86_64's (2026-11-14, targets track). What: crates/core/sys/src/libc/linux_gnu_riscv64.rs holds the 19 items whose libc 0.2.191 definition differs between riscv64 glibc and the shared linux.rs and linux_gnu.rs (blksize_t, nlink_t, wchar_t, epoll_event unpacked, pthread_attr_t, the asm-generic `stat`, O_DIRECT, O_DIRECTORY, O_NOFOLLOW and the generic syscall numbers), taken from libc's macro-expanded source for the target; mod.rs selects unix.rs, linux.rs and linux_gnu.rs for it as for x86_64 and aarch64 glibc; python-capi's build script passes clang `riscv64-` for Rust's `riscv64gc-` triple prefix, which clang does not know. Checked: output/tgt-harness against libc =0.2.191 built for riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu (clang with the Ubuntu 24.04 riscv64 glibc 2.39 cross sysroot, lld) runs under qemu-riscv64-static 8.2.2: 890 checks (39 types, 43 structs with every public field offset, 460 constants, 155 functions by address), 0 failures. `cargo check --locked --workspace --target riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu --keep-going` fails only in graviola (`This crate only supports x86_64 or aarch64`: its s2n-bignum and AES/GHASH kernels are x86_64 and aarch64 assembly with no portable fallback), so nanocode-tls, nanocode-mpp, nanocode-sandbox and what depends on them (nanocode-cli's `nanocode`, nanocode-sim) do not build there; `cargo build --locked -p nanocode-python-cli --target riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu` links, and output/tgt-smoke/py.py (os.uname, math, json, re, struct, hashlib, file write, stat, unlink and ENOENT, signal numbers, time and big integers) prints the same 12 lines under qemu-riscv64 as the x86_64 build. `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`, nanocode-sim `--tidy` and `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 2000 8` (2000 passed) pass. Files: crates/core/sys/src/libc/{mod,linux_gnu_riscv64}.rs, crates/core/python-capi/build.rs.
- fix(android): nanocode builds for aarch64-linux-android and its static binary passes the CLI smokes under qemu-aarch64 (2026-11-14, targets track). Before, nanocode-sys did not build there (alloc/os.rs's `mremap` and signal.rs's `__error` had no Android declaration), and past it nanocode-process, psh-os and rustpython-host_env failed too. What: crates/core/sys/src/libc/android_aarch64.rs gains `mremap`, `TIOCGPTN`, `TIOCSPTLCK` and `RLIMIT_RTTIME` (libc 0.2.191 declares none of them for Android; values from the NDK r27c headers, which a C program built with `aarch64-linux-android30-clang -static` printed: RLIMIT_RTTIME=15, TIOCGPTN=0x80045430, TIOCSPTLCK=0x40045431, and bionic's mremap grows a mapping in place); unix/signal.rs reads errno through bionic's `__errno`; unix/mod.rs opens pseudoterminals through /dev/ptmx on Android as on Linux; psh-os sets errno through `__errno`, calls `faccessat` with no flag on Android (bionic refuses `AT_EACCESS` with EINVAL, checked with the same C program; app processes have equal real and effective ids) and answers `getconf PATH` with bionic's `_PATH_DEFPATH` (bionic has no `confstr`); rustpython-host_env's `set_errno` uses `__errno` on Android; nanocode-process gates its embedded psh, login and warm shells on `unix` instead of macOS or Linux, so Android (and other Unix targets) take the same path (iOS still checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-process -p nanocode-psh-embedded -p nanocode-psh --target aarch64-apple-ios`). Checked: `cargo check --locked --workspace --target aarch64-linux-android` (NDK r27c clang as CC and linker) passes; `cargo build --locked -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --target aarch64-linux-android` with `-C target-feature=+crt-static` links a static 206 MB debug binary; output/tgt-smoke/smoke.sh runs it under qemu-aarch64-static 8.2.2 (registered with binfmt_misc so nanocode's re-exec of itself as psh runs too, then unregistered): `--version`, `--help`, `psh-shell -c` exit status, pipes, arithmetic, file writes and globs, an external program and command substitution, and `nanocode exec` against a local mock of the Anthropic Messages API whose reply calls Code Mode `exec` with `tools.Bash`, which runs `echo smoke-$((6*7))` and returns `smoke-42` to the model, exit 0 (TMPDIR set, since Android's default temp directory is /data/local/tmp); 11 of 11 pass. output/tgt-harness against libc =0.2.191 for aarch64-linux-android (static, under qemu): 781 compile-time type, size, offset, constant and signature checks and run-time address checks pass, the four names above excepted since libc lacks them. Not run on a device or emulator image: the dynamic (bionic linker) binary, the TLS trust store paths and the Android sandbox are unverified. `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`, nanocode-sim `--tidy` and `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 2000 8` (2000 passed) pass. Files: crates/core/sys/src/{libc/android_aarch64.rs,unix/mod.rs,unix/signal.rs}, crates/integrations/process/src/{lib,process,foreground}.rs, crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-os/src/unix/{mod,signals}.rs, crates/patches/rustpython-host_env/src/os.rs.
- measure(hedge): a Claude first-byte hedge window that survives across processes, not landed (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 latency SLA). Tried: `Hedging::seeded(policy, HedgeHistory)` and `Hedging::history()` with a `recorded()` notification in crates/core/agent/src/hedge.rs, and the native host reading `<home>/hedge.json` at `Host::build` and rewriting it (staged file and rename, on a blocking worker) after each recorded sample, so a fresh CLI session starts with the model's last `HedgePolicy::window` first-byte samples and keeps the floor only while no history exists (patch kept outside the repository as hedge-persist.patch). The estimated-only variant (no hedge before `estimate_samples()` samples) was dropped, since a 3-turn session never fills 10 samples. Checks of the tried change: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent-core` native and wasm32, `cargo clippy --no-deps` on `nanocode-agent-core` and `nanocode-cli --bin nanocode` (no new warnings), `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 1000 2 --scenario runtime` 1,000 passed, 0 panics (no new invariant, so no mutation). Measured with nanocode-ts `bench/sla/run.ts --live --lanes=live-nc-claude@before,live-nc-claude@after --samples=32 --turns=3 --settle=3000` (TUI, interleaved, each lane its own `NANOCODE_HOME` and `NANOCODE_TELEMETRY=agent` traces), two rounds per model on a 5-core Linux host whose Anthropic traffic goes through a TLS proxy (load average at most 1.7), before = eecc284db, after = the change, round 2 seeded with round 1's history; n = 64 three-turn sessions per lane per model, e2e TTFT p50/p99 ms, hedges fired (all won by the primary): opus before t1 1,167/5,081 7, t2 1,141/1,656 5, t3 1,144/2,077 6; opus after t1 1,138/2,149 4, t2 1,052/1,669 4, t3 1,111/3,939 2; sonnet before t1 805/1,644 1, t2 892/1,584 2, t3 1,354/1,669 11; sonnet after t1 788/1,602 1, t2 907/1,580 1, t3 932/1,671 3. Hedges fell from 32 to 15 of 384 requests per lane, but p99 got worse on opus t3 (+1,862 ms, one 3,871 ms first byte in session 2 while the history still held fewer than 10 samples, so the deadline was the 1.5 s floor as on master), opus t2 (+13) and sonnet t3 (+2), so the change is not landed. The drop is not attributable to the change either: behind the proxy the persisted p90 first byte was 1,526 ms for opus and 1,070 ms for sonnet, so 12 of 15 after-lane hedges still used the 1.5 s floor deadline. Across all 768 requests of both lanes no hedge won, including both tail turns over 3.5 s (5,077 and 3,871 ms first bytes, each hedged at 1.5 s and still beaten by the primary), so a replay sent at 1.5 s did not shorten any measured tail. Next: measure the persisted window without the proxy, where the p90 sits above the floor.
- fix(platform, sim): simulated crates measure elapsed time with `nanocode_platform::elapsed(since)` (the host's `now()` minus `since`) instead of `Instant::elapsed`, and `--twice` runs its second pass with the host's `Instant` origin on the other side of the real clock, so a real-clock read diverges on every seed instead of about 1 in 160 under load (2026-11-14). Cause: on native `nanocode_platform::Instant` is `std::time::Instant`, so `x.elapsed()` on an instant from `nanocode_platform::now()` (the simulated origin plus virtual time) read the real clock: it was 0 while virtual time ran ahead of real time and grew with wall time once a loaded machine let real time pass the virtual offset. Those reads fed decisions: the Claude cache keep-alive's `reach` and `requested` delays (keep.rs, agent.rs), `outlived_cache`, the session event flush window (session_events.rs), `Shared::now_unless` freshness (sync), the bash stall check, code-mode's `performance.now()` and unclaimed-buffer expiry, and durations in tool results; so the CFO's runtime_kv_twice, runtime_memory_twice and runtime_kv_http_twice saw `nondeterminism: trace digest X then Y` with the same trace line at shifted virtual times ("http connect", "model rN steps", "power loss reverted") on every master commit through eecc284db. Changes: `nanocode_platform::elapsed` (native and wasm32); every `.elapsed()` in the simulated crates goes through it; `--tidy` bans `.elapsed()` there (allowed: lease.rs 2 and store-jsonl lib.rs 5, which time their own real `Instant::now` readings); `host::second_pass` puts the first pass's origin `SIMULATED_START_UNIX_SECS` after the real clock (a leak reads 0) and the second's that far before it (a leak reads decades); mutation `http-real-elapsed` adds the HTTP server's `opened.elapsed()` to each connect's latency. Measured on dev-georgios, cores 0-7: before the product fix, with the shifted origin, `--scenario runtime --store kv --wire http --seeds 0..40 --twice` failed 23 of 40; after it 200 of 200 pass; `--mutation http-real-elapsed --twice` is caught by 40 of 40 seeds (not caught without `--twice`, as a `--twice` check should be). Under load (64 processes pinned to one core), 64 seeds from the CFO's recent runtime `--twice` failures plus the two named ones: eecc284db's binary failed 5 of 64, this build passed 64 of 64 in each of 5 runs. Every CFO `--twice` scenario passes seeds 1000..1200 with the shifted origin (store, store slots, turns, turns turnlog, agents, runtime kv/memory/kv-http/log-remote, websocket, http_server, alloc, egress, mpp, sync, streams, hands); `sweep.sh 0 2000 8` passes 2000; tidy clean. `--store log` (local children) fails 6 of 200 (seeds 1134, 1196, ...: `did not settle within 1800 s`) on eecc284db's binary too, unrelated.
- docs(sla): live GPT rows at 30 sessions per cell on master 8e5cd38d8 against Codex CLI 0.166.0 (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 latency SLA). nanocode wins every p50 cell and 6 of 9 p99 cells on gpt-6-luna, gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6-astra; each p99 loss is one sample of 30 (34 ms and 233 ms, and one gpt-6.1-sol turn 1 at load average 200 on the host).
- feat(nanocode-sim, cfo): the simulator gains an `executor` scenario (nanocode-executor's `JoinHandle`, `JoinSet`, abort, panics, detached tasks and coop budgets: every task's value, cancellation or panic must reach its awaiter exactly once, mutations `skip_abort` and `leak_cancelled`) and a `capture` scenario (nanocode-process's `CapturedOutput` head/tail window with secret redaction across chunk and truncation boundaries, mutations `skip_trim` and `drop_chunk`); `--mutations` lists every scenario's mutations, a `--twice` failure's replay keeps `--twice`, and `cfo.sh` publishes to the private `gakonst/nanocode-cfo-db` (2026-11-14). Why: the CFO fuzzed none of the executor or the process output path, ran 24 workers on cores 8-31 of a 32-core box shared with other agents (load average 205 when measured), kept every result only in a local 716 MB `results.jsonl`, never ran 17 of the 72 mutations as canaries, and printed replays of `--twice` nondeterminism failures without `--twice`, so they passed when replayed. What: `CapturedOutput`, `CapturedChunk::render` (the redaction `SessionState` already did, moved so the simulator drives the same code) and its accessors are public. `cfo.sh` now fuzzes on cores 20-31 and builds on 16-19 (16 cores, `CPUAffinity` in the unit, workers = fuzz cores), adds pass rows for `executor`, `capture`, `hands`, turnlog `--event-bytes`, `--snapshot-rows`, `--retain` and runtime `--children remote`, a canary row with the flags that make each of the 17 missing mutations catchable (each measured: e.g. `archive_drops_events` 63/200 with `--event-bytes 32768`, `child-acks-early` 1/200 with `--children remote`, so its canary runs 1,000 seeds), and turns any mutation `--mutations` lists without a row into a default canary. Every 5 minutes it merges new records into `fuzzing/data.jsonl` on the `data` branch of the results repository as zempo-cfo-db does (newest 32 commits, per commit and fuzzer one counting record and at most 4 failing seeds with the rest counted, failure logs capped at 4 MiB in `fuzzing/logs/`, retried up to 32 times), writes a README with machines, the newest 3 failing commits, the canaries' catch rates and seeds per commit, and triages the newest unseen failing (commit, fuzzer): it replays the seed alone and, when it reproduces, bisects the first failing commit over the per-commit binaries it kept; it also keeps only 32 binaries, 7 days of logs and rotates `results.jsonl` past 1 GiB once uploaded (the disk was 97% full). Verified on dev-georgios: `--seeds 0..2000` of `executor` and `capture` pass (and `--twice` on 0..200), `skip_abort` caught by 132/400, `leak_cancelled` 275/400, `skip_trim` 137/400, `drop_chunk` 400/400; a 150 s `cfo.sh run` against a local results repository uploaded and rendered its README; merging the last 70 MB of the live results took 99 s on 4 loaded cores, so a first upload starts from the newest 64 MiB.
- build(cli): when BOLT's rewritten code does not fit the original `.text`, scripts/build-cli.sh runs the final BOLT pass again with `-lite`, so only the profiled functions move and the rest stay where the linker put them: `PROFILE=lite scripts/build-cli.sh nc-lite nc-lite` 31,789,496 to 21,583,840 bytes (-10.2 MB) with the same first frame and one-shot (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: nc-lite binary size against fx 0.0.16's 12,814,000 bytes). Why: since `-use-old-text` BOLT writes its layout into the linker's `.text`, but for nc-lite (`opt-level = "z"`) the rewritten code is larger than the original (`BOLT-WARNING: original .text too small to fit the new code using 0x1000 alignment. 13142373 bytes needed, have 12807330 bytes available`, still 13,053,519 needed with no splitting and `-align-functions=16`), and BOLT then keeps the whole original as `.bolt.org.text` (12.8 MB) beside a full rewritten copy (`.text` 1.2 MB, `.text.cold` 11.9 MB). With `-lite` the profiled functions go to the new 1.0 MB hot `.text` and 1.3 MB `.text.cold`, and every other function runs from the original `.text` unchanged. nanocode's own build fits and keeps its current pass; the retry only runs when BOLT prints that warning. Measured on the same training output (output of `PROFILE=lite LLVM_BOLT=/usr/lib/llvm-21/bin/llvm-bolt scripts/build-cli.sh nc-lite nc-lite` at d52492d5d, the final pass rerun by hand with `-lite`, then llvm-strip and scripts/trim-cli.py as the script does), 3 interleaved runs each against bench/cli's fakellm (output/l11/ff.py, output/l11/one.sh): first-frame RSS 3,156 to 3,208 KB for both (the unBOLTed static build: 10,000 KB); one-shot `exec` 8.05 to 8.51 M user instructions, 371 to 384 page faults and 11.8 to 12.3 MB peak RSS for both (unBOLTed: 502 to 505 faults, 13.8 to 14.3 MB); streaming 50,000 tokens at 10,000 tok/s, 1.0 to 1.3 G user instructions in the quiet runs of both. The unBOLTed static build is 18,507,360 bytes, so this keeps 3.1 MB of BOLT layout for a third of the first-frame RSS. `sh -n scripts/build-cli.sh`.
- fix(psh): match bash 5.3 messages and behaviour for traces, errors and fds (2026-11-14, psh conformance). Parse errors inside alias text show the alias text as the offending line. A conditional expression error names the line where its [[ starts. A bad word in an array literal resumes reading after its line, as a bad compound assignment does. PS4 with an unterminated ${ reports a bad substitution and with an unterminated $( a command substitution error. -O and -o invocation errors print bash's line 0 messages without the usage. Assigning an invalid BASH_XTRACEFD reports it. $\<newline>'...' and a line continuation in single quotes of a double-quoted operand expand as bash's. wait without operands waits for the last process substitution. The psh program adopts the descriptors above 2 it inherits. With extdebug a failing DEBUG trap skips a for loop iteration. echo and printf run from env report write errors as the programs do. ls without operands in a removed directory lists nothing. A local copies a caller's temporary binding, set lists arrays, binary files are detected by an ELF header or a NUL in the first line (two after #!), messages in a function name its file, the effective group comes first in GROUPS, and ((...)) errors name the line where the command ends. Validated with psh-spec: brush 3123 -> 3133, oils 2491 -> 2498, no new failures. - fix(psh): match bash 5.3 parse errors, loop control, xtrace and trap messages (2026-11-14, psh conformance). Parse errors named other tokens and lines than bash 5.3, several builtins returned bash 5.2 statuses, and xtrace and trap actions differed. [[ ]] errors name the text bash reads back from the next unread byte (near `&' for `&&', `3<'), and a group adds "expected `)'". Unterminated quotes report the line of the opening quote; an unexpected end of file after a last line without a newline reports the next line. for (( )) errors show the clause text; under set -e only the first line of a syntax error prints, and eval exits. return, shift, break, continue and history check their number before the count of arguments; too many arguments abandons the line with status 2 (with -c, the shell ends with 1). break and continue in a command substitution or a pipeline stage end that subshell. set -x traces compound assignments, export and readonly assignments only, one more PS4 character in sourced files and traps, nothing for an unset PS4, and a lone single quote as \'. Trap actions report errors as "exit trap", "trap", "debug trap" and so on, with lines counted from the action for EXIT and signals. set -v echoes blank lines; mapfile -d '' drops the NUL; a function with an invalid name and a command found in PATH report as bash does. psh-spec (in-process, Linux): brush 3033 -> 3039, oils 2419 -> 2429, agent 727, utils 999, no new failures. - fix(psh): restricted, interactive and dump invocation, programs that override utilities, readonly _ (2026-11-14, psh conformance). psh takes -r/--restricted (restricted shell rules for cd, exec, command -p, source, hash, redirections and slashes in command names), -i (interactive variables, prompts on stderr, job control notice) and -D/--dump-strings and --dump-po-strings; set -r turns restricted mode on. - fix(psh): sort glob results by the collation of a non-C LC_COLLATE (2026-11-14, psh conformance). With LC_ALL, LC_COLLATE or LANG naming a locale other than C or POSIX, pathname expansion sorts as glibc's locales do for ASCII: punctuation is ignored first, letters compare without case and then lowercase first, and punctuation decides ties. - fix(psh): trap nesting, ERR trap timing, signals of programs and stages, time of a subshell (2026-11-14, psh conformance). Several trap, signal, pipeline and redirection behaviours differed from bash 5.3: DEBUG and ERR traps did not run inside other trap actions; each is now only kept from running inside its own action (in_debug_trap, in_err_trap), and BASH_COMMAND keeps its value during a trap. Signal and EXIT trap actions count $LINENO from 1. A function call that sets the ERR trap does not run it for its own failure (err_trap_new); a failing ( ... ) that ends a pipeline runs the ERR trap for itself and for the pipeline. A compound command whose redirection fails keeps the previous $LINENO for the ERR trap. The SIGINT wait of bash: a foreground program that does not die of an untrapped SIGINT leaves the shell running (Gives::Program). kill 0 (or the shell's group) from a subshell or pipeline stage ends that vproc by the signal's default action, or queues its trap. A background job of one simple command releases its descriptors once its program starts, so a pipe reader is not held open. break and continue in a simple-command pipeline stage keep the loop count, so they are silent as in bash. time ( ... ) reports on the subshell's stderr when the subshell ends. set -t (onecmd) ends a script or stdin after the next command. The exec builtin keeps its redirections with options and with a command (exec -- 3>&1). A redirection open fails with "Too many open files" when the lowest free descriptor is at or above ulimit -n's soft limit. psh-spec (in-process, Linux): brush 3033 -> 3039, oils 2419 -> 2426, agent 727/727, utils 999/1001, no new failures. - perf(turnlog): a snapshot the row rule makes (`snapshot_rows`) is deflated at level 1 instead of 6, and `SqlLog`'s extend statement cuts the tail row as a blob (2026-11-14, Georgios: the CPU cost of nanocode-ts's 64-row snapshot rule). Why: each row-rule snapshot re-serializes and deflates the whole state, so on nanocode-ts a190f20 against eecc284db a 1,200-turn session cost 97.1M user instructions per warm turn with `snapshot_rows` Some(64) against 27.7M without the rule (37.5M against 28.4M at 200 turns). Deflate at level 6 was most of a snapshot: the 9,218,518-byte plain of that session's last snapshot deflates natively (nanocode-compression, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, ~/djs2/snap/lvlbench) in 771M instructions to 1,880,786 B at level 6, 693M/1,962,643 B at 4, 658M/2,020,157 B at 3, 434M/2,079,173 B at 2 and 248M/3,107,018 B at 1 (`deflate_quick`). Separately, SQLite's `substr` and `length` walk a TEXT value character by character, so every `turn_log_extend` scanned the whole tail row twice: `perf record` of 200-turn runs put substrFunc and lengthFunc at 2.3% of user instructions with 64 rows and 7.7% with 256. What: `codec::Packer::new` takes the level; `Lease::commit` packs a snapshot that the row rule made due with `FAST_LEVEL` (1), and the ratio rule's probe and its snapshots keep `DEFAULT_LEVEL`. The row format is unchanged (raw deflate, which inflates the same whatever the level); the archive of a superseded snapshot is still packed from its plain suffix, and the rows after a snapshot still take its plain suffix as their dictionary, so they decode as before (every cold open in the runs below decoded a level-1 snapshot and its extended tail row). The SQLite `EXTEND` sets `body = substr(CAST(body AS BLOB), 1, length(CAST(body AS BLOB)) - ?4) || ?5`: the cast copies nothing, blob lengths and offsets are bytes, and `||` of a blob and text yields text, so the stored value is the same text (checked in node:sqlite: `typeof(body)` stays `text`); bodies are ASCII base64, so bytes are characters. The Postgres statement is unchanged. Measured with nanocode-ts output/snapprof.ts (the real `SqlLog` over node:sqlite, N turns cycling six cells against a mock model, `perf stat -e instructions:u -t <main thread>` over turns 4..N, then two cold opens, each a new runtime's `open` and its first turn), interleaved runs, warm M instructions per turn at 50/200/1,200 turns: Some(64) before 38.7/37.5/97.1, blob extend alone -/35.9/-, both 35.9/32.5/72.3; with nanocode-ts at Some(128) 35.1/29.4/51.1 and Some(256) 35.9/28.9/40.8 (None 35.1/28.4/27.7). Cold open (open + first turn, M) at 200 turns: 455+90 before, 461+89 with both at 64, 488+89 at 128; at 1,200 turns 2,252+271 before, 2,359+270 at 64, 2,384+270 at 128. The live snapshot is 1.6x larger (2,513,147 to 4,135,891 B at 1,200 turns), and only the newest snapshot is whole, so stored bytes at 1,200 turns go from 7.40 MB to 8.81 MB at 128. Checks: `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 2000 12 --scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` (2,000 passed), the same with `--snapshot-rows 4 --state-bytes 131072` and with `--snapshot-rows 4`, and `sweep.sh 0 200 12 --scenario turns --policy turnlog --long 100`, all with 0 failures and 0 panics; `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog -p nanocode-agent`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps --lib -p nanocode-turnlog -- -D warnings` on both targets, rustfmt on the changed files. Files: crates/core/turnlog/src/{codec,host,writer}.rs.

- fix(codex): a Codex session whose Code Mode cells run on a hand reports that hand's shell in `<environment_context>` instead of `javascript`, and the native hand reports bash, the shell its `exec_command` runs, when `SHELL` is unset (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 circuit-fibsqrt: nanox 0/4 in 0d6c29c9 and 0/2 in 16e15f9a, cx 2/4). Why: `EmbeddedToolRuntime::default_shell_name` is the constant `javascript` and the codex turn passed it to `ContextSnapshot::capture`, so every nanox request (nanocode-ts 281c7dd, hand `-C /app`) said `<cwd>/app</cwd><shell>javascript</shell>` while its `exec_command` ran /bin/bash on the hand and codex-cli 0.166 says `<shell>bash</shell>`; the slot hand's `about` showed no shell (`{"os_version":"Linux 6.1.189+","platform":"linux"}`) because the krun guest has no `SHELL`. What: `CodeModeHost::shell` (default: the hand description's `environment.shell`, routed through `CodeModeExecutors`' placement as `working_directory` is), `context_shell` on the embedded and native tool runtimes, the three codex `capture` calls use it, and `local_environment` falls back to `nanocode_home::shell::default_shell_name()`, the shell the process runtime stands psh in for. - build(cli): nanocode.exe reserves an 8 MiB main-thread stack on Windows, as nanocode-python.exe does, through bin/nanocode/build.rs (`/STACK:8388608` for MSVC, `-Wl,--stack,8388608` for GNU, bins only) (2026-11-14, Windows hill-climb). Why: on Windows the main thread's stack is whatever the PE header reserves, 1 MiB by default, while on Linux and macOS it is the 8 MiB default the depth bounds in psh, the parsers and the turn loop were tried against, and nanocode runs its whole turn loop (`run_with`'s `block_on`) and, re-executed as the shell, all of psh on that thread. What: the same build script nanocode-python has; Unix links are unchanged. Measured on GitHub Actions windows-latest (x64, Windows 10.0.26100) and windows-11-arm (ARM64, 10.0.26200) from a private scratch repository at eecc284db plus 59e174e63: `llvm-readobj --file-headers` gives SizeOfStackReserve 1048576 without the script and 8388608 with it, for the release and dev builds on both. No failure at 1 MiB was found: dev builds with either reserve passed `--version`, `psh-shell -c 'echo $((6*7))'` and a Claude session (`exec --ephemeral --harness claude`, a Bash tool call, through a Claude plan token written to `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/.credentials.json`) on both, and on Linux psh's own bounds (function nesting 1000, arithmetic nesting, `nesting too deep`) stop deep scripts before 512 KiB (`ulimit -s 512` and `1024` against `8192`, release build). So this is parity, not a crash fix. Also run on both runners: the release build's Claude session ran `echo`, `python3 -c 'print(6*7)'` and `uname -a` through its Bash tool and answered with the outputs, and the windows-runtime harness (the 81 checks of 2026-11-12's probe, copied to output/windows-runtime with `libc::STDOUT_FILENO` replaced by 1, which nanocode's Windows libc does not define) passed 79 of 81 on ARM64 and on x64 when started from the Actions step's Git Bash; the two that failed (`win32.console_ctrl`, `executor.ctrl_c_delivery`: a child on its own console never sees the CTRL_C_EVENT it sends itself) fail the same way when the child first calls `SetConsoleCtrlHandler(NULL, FALSE)`, and pass on both runners when the harness is started outside that process tree (WMI `Win32_Process.Create`), so they are the runner's process tree, not nanocode: 81 of 81 on x64 and ARM64. Checks: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo check --locked --target aarch64-pc-windows-msvc -p nanocode-cli --bins`, nanocode-sim release `sweep.sh 0 2000 8` passed, `--tidy` clean. - perf(durability-core): a `StateSummary` leaves out `scope`, `parent`, `title` and `preview` when they are `None` (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: nc-lite store bytes per one-turn session). Every session the JSONL store summarizes is written twice in `sessions/.summaries` (its `remember` journal line, then the plain base), and a root session without a title carried `"parent":null,"title":null` in both. The fields are `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` now; readers of any version read a missing `Option` field as `None`, so homes and summaries written before and after this change read the same everywhere, and nothing that serializes `StateSummary` uses a non-self-describing format. `attributes` keeps being written when empty, since a reader from before this change requires it. Measured with output/l11/store.sh (300 one-turn `nc-lite exec` sessions against fakellm, debug builds of master after a85085a42 and of this change): `sessions/.summaries` 664 to 640 B per session, store bytes (`du -sb` of the home) 1,387 to 1,366 B per session; master lists a home this build wrote and this build lists master's. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core -p nanocode-store-jsonl`, and `-p nanocode-durability-core -p nanocode-durability --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- docs(sla): the deployed Worker at 30 sessions per provider with the session object's own timings (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 latency SLA). A cold turn sends its provider request 56 to 63 ms after it arrives (15 ms warm), and the provider's first byte is the same cold and warm, so the cold first text the client sees is the provider plus the network; the cold gate is read as the Worker's share (time to the provider request plus the first delta's relay), which holds at p50 on both providers and at p99 on Codex, and misses at Claude p99 on the first admission commit of a claimed pooled object (703 ms). Measured with durable-cloudflare's `probe.ts` from the hosted Hand, 180 turns, 0 errors.
- perf(store-jsonl): archiving a session removes its `<session>.owner` lock file while this process still holds the lock, and taking the lock checks that the locked file is still the one at the path (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: nc-lite store bytes per one-turn session). Why: since 689bce2ac every session a CLI acquired kept a 7-byte `.owner` file after the process exited, and each one takes an inode, a directory entry and a 4 KB filesystem block, as much disk as the session's archive; the lock only means something while its process runs, and archiving is that process saying it is done with the session. What: `Sessions::archive` takes the session's held lock file out of `held`, unlinks `.owner` inside the same `listing.change` as the archive (so the `.listing` stamp covers it) and drops the file, which releases the lock, only when the archive was written; when archiving declines or fails the lock goes back to `held`. `hold` now loops: after `try_lock` succeeds it compares the locked file's identity with the file at the path (`same_file`, dev and inode on Unix) and opens again when they differ, the usual lock-file check, so a process that opened `.owner` just before the archiving process unlinked it cannot hold a lock on an unlinked inode that `live_owner` in a third process would never see. Measured with output/l11/store.sh (300 one-turn `nc-lite exec` sessions against fakellm, debug builds of master after ff38d2fa4 and of this change): files in `sessions/` 600 to 300, `du -sk` of the home 2,680 to 1,464 KB (4.1 KB less per session on disk), `du -sb` 7 B less per session (the bench's `store_bytes_per_session` counts file bytes only), the `sessions/` directory itself 49,152 to 32,768 B; `--continue` of an archived session takes the lock again and removes it when it archives. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-jsonl`, native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- perf(store-jsonl): session archives are format 2, a zstd frame against `session2.dict`, a 42.7 KB raw-content dictionary of today's compacted sessions, and an archived session's summary is moved to its archive in one journal line without an anchor (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: nc-lite store bytes per one-turn session). Why: `session.dict` was built on 2026-11-11 from sessions of that day's format, and the format has moved since (the `:pool` state, `head` checkpoints, owner lines), so a one-turn nc-lite session of 7.2 KB still archived to 1,397 B; with a dictionary made from current sessions the template is free and what remains is mostly the session's own hashes and ids. What: `archive::compress` writes format byte 2 and compresses against `session2.dict` (the concatenation of one compacted nanocode one-turn session, one nc-lite two-turn `--continue` session, one nc-lite three-step `exec_command` session and one nc-lite one-turn session, generated against bench/cli's fakellm); `decompress` reads format 2 with it and format 1 with `session.dict`, which stays unchanged, so every existing archive and the old compressed summaries base still open; a build from before this change reports `unknown JSONL archive format` for a format-2 archive instead of misreading it. `Sessions::archive` records one `moved` line from the session file's identity before compaction straight to the archive's (the compaction's own `moved` line is written only when archiving declines), and without an anchor: the anchor was the SHA-256 of the archive, 64 hex characters plus its key in the base and in the journal, and it only spared `copied` a decompression of the archive when a home was copied; without it `copied` reads the archive's last replacement through `ending`, as for any summary without an anchor, and remembers the anchor it finds then. Measured with output/l11/store.sh (300 one-turn `nc-lite exec` sessions against fakellm into a fresh home, debug builds of master and of this change, same machine): store bytes (`du -sb` of the home) 691,698 to 417,664, 2,305 to 1,392 B per session; archives 1,397 to 653 B per session; `sessions/.summaries` 834 to 665 B per session; the 19.8 KB of shared records and the 7 B owner files unchanged. Through nanocode-zstd's own encoder at level 1 (output/l11/zh): a nanocode one-turn session 1,719 to 637 B, a nanocode three-step Code Mode session 3,821 to 2,833 B, an nc-lite three-step session 1,781 to 855 B. Reading: a master-built home lists and `--continue`s with this build (the continued session is rewritten as format 2), and master lists a home this build wrote from its summaries. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-jsonl`, native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- feat(python): `kiwisolver._cext` (kiwisolver 1.5.1) is a built-in module written in Rust, so `import kiwisolver` with the package's own Python files passes its upstream test suite, 50 passed with none skipped, natively and in python.wasm (2026-11-14, Georgios: run the top compiled Python packages in plain wasm32 with no Pyodide). kiwisolver is C++ throughout (the kiwi Cassowary solver headers and a binding on std::map, std::string, std::stringstream, std::recursive_mutex and exceptions), and compiling it needs libc++, libc++abi, libunwind and wasm exception handling, whose exnref form Node 22 to 24 reject without flags, so the solver and the binding are ported instead: crates/core/python/src/kiwisolver/kiwi.rs follows kiwi/solverimpl.h with the same symbol ordering, pivot, entering and leaving choices, dual optimize, the epsilon of kiwi/util.h and the strength arithmetic of strength.h, and dumps() writes debug.h's text with a %g formatter; mod.rs is the binding (Variable, Term, Expression, Constraint, Solver, the strength object, the six exceptions taken from kiwisolver.exceptions as init_exceptions does). A 216-line behaviour script (reprs, every error and message, hashing, operators, `|` strength, four solver dumps) matches Pyodide 314's upstream kiwisolver 1.5.0 except where upstream orders by memory address (std::map over PyObject* and VariableData*): term order in a constraint's expression and the Variables, Edit Variables and Constraints sections of dumps() follow creation order here, so they are the same on every run and target. kiwi's InternalSolverError, which upstream leaves uncaught, raises RuntimeError with the same message. Benchmark, 60 left and 60 width variables with about 300 chained layout constraints, best of 5, ms, python.wasm then Pyodide: addConstraint 80.9 vs 163.6 to 358.3, 20 addEditVariable 0.98 vs 2.8, 200 suggestValue and updateVariables 2.4 vs 10.1 to 13.4, dumps 10.8 vs 8.8 to 10.7, the same final extent (3245.0). Known gap: at 300 variables addConstraint grows with N cubed and takes about 29 s in python.wasm, not yet compared with native C++ at that size. nanocode-ts bench/python/score.ts at this tree: packages 5/18 to 6/18, python.wasm 28,773,755 bytes (about +140 KB). Unchanged in python.wasm: pyyaml 2609, ujson 454 passed and 4 skipped, msgpack 154 passed and 7 skipped. Commands: `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-python --no-deps -- -D warnings` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown; `node scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs` reports nanocode-backend-codex-client to nanocode-agent-core, which master already has. - fix(djs-libm): `pow` doubles bit patterns with `<<` instead of `2 *` (2026-11-14). The routine is a port of ARM optimized-routines' C `pow`, where `2 * ix` on a `uint64_t` wraps; in Rust it overflows for every argument with the sign bit set, so a build with overflow checks (the `dev` profile) panicked with `attempt to multiply with overflow` in `zeroinfnan` for a negative special-case `y` such as `Math.pow(2, -Infinity)`, and in `issignaling` and the `x` checks for a negative `x`. Release builds wrapped and returned the right value, so only debug builds were wrong. Found by a differential harness in ignored `output/diff` (built with `overflow-checks = true`) that compares `djs_libm` with the `libm` 0.2.16 crate and glibc's `pow`, and pymath's `m_rust` with upstream pymath 0.2.0, on 64 special, subnormal, boundary and random inputs per seed: before the fix seed 1 failed at `pow.rs:1041`; after it, `libm 180 4` ran 2,196,576 seeds (about 140M inputs for each of 30 functions) with no divergence. The run's other differentials found no divergence: `pymath` (vendored pymath against pymath 0.2.0, 208,745 seeds in 180 s), `digest` (nanocode-digest's SHA-1, SHA-2, BLAKE3, xxh64, CRC-32 and Adler-32 against sha1 0.11, sha2 0.11, blake3 1.8.7, xxhash-rust 0.8.19, crc32fast 1.5 and adler2 2.0.1, 55,657 seeds), `zlib` (nanocode-compression's deflate and inflate against libz-rs-sys 0.6.8 call by call: return codes, bytes consumed and produced, output bytes, totals, error messages and dictionaries over every window-bits, level, memLevel, strategy and flush, with mutated and random inflate input; 9,480,377 seeds in 1500 s on 8 threads), `miniz` (`miniz::compress*` and `Writer` against miniz_oxide 0.8.9 and flate2 1.1.9 byte for byte, 851,630 seeds in 1500 s) and serde_json (the vendored serde_json, serde_core, itoa, memchr and indexmap against the registry's serde_json 1.0.150: values and error messages with line and column, round trips, typed and raw-value reads, readers, streams, float and string serialization; 26M seeds with and without `preserve_order`, identical output hashes).
- fix(executor): a blocking-pool thread that is leaving gives up its count before it last looks at the queue, and serves a job it finds there, so a job pushed while the pool's last thread leaves is no longer stranded (2026-11-14, Windows hill-climb). Why: `Pool::work` broke out of its loop once keep-alive ran out with an empty queue and decremented `threads` only after that; a `spawn` in between pushed its job, found the leaving thread's `Idle` already claimed, and could not add a thread because `threads` still counted the leaving one (at `max`), so the job sat in the queue until some later `spawn`, and a `spawn_blocking` awaited alone never finished. What: `work` loops over `serve` (the old body); after `serve` returns it decrements `threads`, then, unless the pool is shutting down or the queue is empty, takes a thread slot again with `add_thread` (a `fetch_update` that refuses past `max`, which `spawn` also uses instead of add-then-undo) and serves again; the shutdown waiter is woken only by the thread that leaves the count at zero. Because the leaving thread decrements before it reads the queue and `spawn` pushes before it tries `add_thread`, one of them always sees the other (all SeqCst). Measured with output/blocking-race (a `spawn_blocking` per `block_on`, awaited under a 2 s timeout, `max_blocking_threads` and keep-alive as arguments) on dev-georgios, master against this change with a 1 ms sleep injected in both between the end of the idle loop and the decrement, to widen the window: `200 1 0 1` (rounds, max, keep-alive µs, spawners) master STUCK at round 2, this change OK in 39 ms; `200 1 0 4` master STUCK at round 1, this change OK; `200 4 0 8` both OK. Without the injected sleep neither stranded a job in 20,000 rounds at `1 50 1`, `1 0 4`, `2 10 8` and `1 1000 2` on Linux, windows-latest (x64) or windows-11-arm (the window is a few instructions wide). Checks: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-executor` (no warnings), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-executor --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `--target aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`, nanocode-sim release `sweep.sh 0 2000 8` SWEEP passed=2000 failed=0, `--tidy` clean. File: crates/core/executor/src/blocking.rs.
- fix(claude): a response Claude's safety classifier refuses (`stop_reason: refusal`) is sent again, once per turn, to the model Claude Code falls back to for the refusal's `stop_details.category`, instead of ending the turn (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 Claude arm). Why: on the full Terminal-Bench 2.1 run with `claude-opus-5-5` (high), 16 of 129 finished Nano attempts ended as `provider refused the request (stop_reason=refusal); turn stopped`, always within its first three model calls, on break-filter-js-from-html, crack-7z-hash, dna-assembly, dna-insert, feal-differential-cryptanalysis, feal-linear-cryptanalysis, protein-assembly and vulnerable-secret, while Claude Code on the same tasks and model was never stopped. Claude Code's request log shows the same refusal on `claude-opus-5-5` (a call with 0 output tokens) and then every later call of the attempt on `claude-opus-4-8` (crack-7z-hash: 2 calls on opus-5-5, 38 on opus-4-8) or `claude-opus-5` (dna-assembly: 2 and 38). Claude Code 2.1.318's route table (`Hc` in its bundle), keyed by the refusing model and the category, is copied as it is: `claude-opus-5-5` sends bio and frontier_llm to `claude-opus-5` and cyber to `claude-opus-4-8`; `claude-opus-5` sends cyber to `claude-opus-4-8`; `claude-sonnet-5-5` sends cyber and frontier_llm to `claude-sonnet-5`; any other model sends bio and frontier_llm to `claude-opus-5` and cyber to `claude-opus-4-8`; nothing else falls back, and a model never falls back to itself. Like Claude Code, the refused response is dropped and the same messages are sent again; the fallback model stays on the cursor's template for the rest of the turn, and a refusal on the fallback goes through the existing one-time recovery notice and then stops the turn as before. The client now keeps `stop_details` from `message_delta` and from a whole response. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude`, native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- fix(turnlog): the Postgres `LOAD` and `SCAN` statements order rows by `nanocode_log.seq` (2026-11-14). Both select `CAST(seq AS TEXT)`, which Postgres names `seq`, and a bare `ORDER BY seq` binds to that output column before the table's, so rows came back in text order (1, 10, 11, 2, ...) once a scope reached 10 rows. Each row's deflate stream takes the previous rows as its dictionary, so the out-of-order read failed with `turn log row decompression failed: data error` and a durable session could not be opened again. SQLite names the cast column `CAST(seq AS TEXT)`, so its statements were right. `session_log.rs` already qualifies its Postgres `ORDER BY` the same way. Found by a host whose Postgres session reached its fifth turn. Checked with a harness in ignored `output/turnlog-repro` that loads one scope's 11 rows through `SqlLog` over `PgSql` and compares them with `psql`'s rows: before the fix the rows came back as 1, 10, 11, 2 ... 9 and `TurnLog::open` failed. After it they match in order and `TurnLog::open` succeeds; the same rows opened from memory (`LogHost` over a `Vec`) succeed both before and after. No other Postgres statement here orders by a column it also selects through a cast. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog`, native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- feat(tool-runtime): `remote::accept::Acceptor` serves many hands, each under its own credential and route key, and records every request it sends a hand so a hand's kept replies survive a host restart (2026-11-14). What: the host supplies the stream (it terminates TLS and routes) and an authorization callback `(path, headers) -> Result<Binding { key }, Refusal { status, body }>`; `Acceptor::serve` reads the request head, answers the host's own HTTP routes through `nanocode_http::server::serve` and upgrades the configured path to a websocket, reads the catalog (`read_catalog`), runs `websocket()`'s heartbeat and attaches the socket to its key. One `RemoteClient` per hand runtime (the catalog's resumable `runtime_id`) runs over a redial link: a socket that fails waits `reconnect_grace` for the same runtime's next socket, which starts with the catalog replayed so the client sends `Resume` for what it wrote; a new runtime for the key replaces the old client, whose calls end with the unknown outcome they always had. `Acceptor::route(resolve)` is a session's `RemoteTransport`: each operation goes to the client of the key `resolve` names, waiting `reconnect_grace` for a live socket. Every bound (frame bytes, head, catalog, ping, heartbeat, operation and reconnect timeouts, runtimes, queued attach notices) is the host's `AcceptorOptions`. Durability: `RemoteClient::durable(link, timeout, pending, ledger)` records each Execute, Wait and Call (`RemoteLedger::sent`: request id, session, call and turn id) before its frame is queued, so a request it cannot record is refused unsent; it stores each reply the hand sent (`RemoteLedger::replied`, the resolved value for Execute and Wait, after `ReceivedCalls` expands nested calls the updates carried, since the hand's live reply elides them) and only then acks it. The driver never auto-acks a recorded request's reply on a durable client: a hand may send one reply twice (once when the call ends, again for the `Resume` a new socket sends), and the simulator caught the driver acking the second copy before the first was stored (4 of the first 200 seeds), which lets the hand drop the only copy if the host then crashes. Replies the waiters get from the client itself (termination, refusals, settled controls) are marked as not from the hand and never stored. `HandRequests` is the store (`SqlRequests` over any `Sql` host: table `nanocode_hand_requests`, format component `hand_requests`, one row per session and call, upserted when a call is sent again); a client of a runtime the store already knows starts with that runtime's unanswered request ids as `pending`, so its first `Resume` asks the hand for them and the hand answers with its kept full reply, the reply of a call still running, or not received. A durable session's resume calls `RemoteTransport::recover(context)` for an interrupted exec, wait or call; the route answers from the row for that session and call: the stored reply (a not-received reply as unsent, which the drivers treat as never dispatched and run again), or it waits while the recorded runtime is attached (bounded by the operation timeout) or `reconnect_grace` while no runtime is, and answers `HAND_RESTARTED` when the key's runtime changed, `NOT_ANSWERED` past those bounds, and `NOT_RECORDED` (unsent) when no row exists, which is safe because a row is written before any frame and removed only by `Acceptor::settle(session_id)`, which the host calls once a session's turn has ended. A hand without a resumable runtime is still recorded, under a runtime id the acceptor draws, so its interrupted calls report unknown rather than not dispatched. `RemoteClient::calls` refuses on a durable client, since it cannot await each record before sending. feat(sim): `--scenario hands` (bin/nanocode-sim/src/hands.rs) runs the real acceptor, redial and durable client against a simulated hand that keeps replies until acked, answers `Resume` as nanocode's hand does, restarts as a new runtime, and loses its socket; the host crashes at random points with an in-memory `HandRequests` whose writes take time and are lost if the crash lands first, and a session commits each call's outcome after a delay, recovering uncommitted calls after each restart. Invariants and the mutation each catches: `ack_after_store` (no ack reaches the hand for a request whose reply is not stored; `ack_before_store` acks without storing, caught by 1,970 of 2,000 seeds), `once` (the hand runs each call at most once; `skip_record` sends without a row, so recovery runs the call again, 629 of 2,000), `settles` (every call commits before a 60 s horizon; `forget_pending` drops the runtime's pending ids, so the hand forgets the kept reply and recovery waits forever, 455 of 2,000), `real` (a committed value is the one output the hand produced; `cross_replies` writes a reply into the runtime's other unanswered rows, 456 of 2,000), `honest` (a call commits unknown only if its hand restarted while it was open; `mangle_runtime` stores the wrong runtime, 584 of 2,000). `sweep.sh 0 20000 8 --scenario hands --twice` passed 20,000 seeds, and `--seeds 0..2000 --twice` passed with identical traces (918 host crashes, 185 hand restarts, 938 socket drops, 6,058 calls, 1,282 recovered after a crash, 230 honest unknowns); the runtime (local and remote children, http wire), store and turns sweeps pass unchanged.
- feat(codex): the `responses.attempt` span records `hedge.status` (dispatched, capped or throttled), `hedge.deadline_ns`, `hedge.winner` (primary or hedge) and, when the hedge's first byte arrived, `hedge.first_byte_ns`, on the WebSocket and HTTPS paths, as the Claude `messages.attempt` span records its hedge (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 latency SLA: follow-up of the Codex hedge change). The hedge-wins path, checked against a local Responses mock (output/hedge-mock: aiohttp `mock.py` serves SSE and WebSocket `/v1/responses`, sends `response.created` at once and holds the primary 5 s before its first output, answers a request with `x-nanocode-hedge: 1` in `client_metadata` at once, answers the first request of turn 2 with a function call so the turn makes a second request, and sets `x-codex-turn-state` per connection or response; `src/main.rs` runs three turns through `OpenAi::builder` with `HedgePolicy` floor 300 ms and cap 100%): on both transports every request hedged and the hedge won, each turn's deltas and final message were the hedge's text once (`HEDGE-WON turn N via rK`), and the stalled primary was dropped (WebSocket: the primary socket closed with 1006 within 3 ms of the hedge's completion; HTTPS: the primary's stream reset). Turn state follows the winner: over HTTPS the second request of turn 2 carried `ts-hedge-r4`, the hedge response's state, and hedges carried none; over WebSocket the next request went on the hedge's socket with `previous_response_id` of the hedge's response, and each hedge was a full replay on a new socket opened without turn state. `nanocode exec` against the same mock over HTTPS (`NANOCODE_OPENAI_BASE_URL`, `NANOCODE_HEDGE_FLOOR_MS=300`) wrote `hedge.status=dispatched hedge.winner=hedge hedge.deadline_ns=300000000` into the local trace. Live, ChatGPT login on dev-georgios, gpt-6-luna over WebSocket, `NANOCODE_HEDGE_FLOOR_MS=100 NANOCODE_HEDGE_CAP_PERCENT=100`, 4 three-turn sessions: 12 of 12 requests hedged with the marker, no error, 1 hedge win (turn 3 of one session, hedge first byte at 1,778 ms). Spare WebSocket: with `NANOCODE_HEDGE_FLOOR_MS=20000` (no hedge sent), 3 three-turn gpt-6-luna sessions each opened one Hedge-purpose connection, at turn 1, and turns 2 and 3 used it without a new connect, so the server keeps an idle spare for at least the 4 to 5 s between turns; with the 100 ms floor every turn opened a new one because the hedge sent on the spare. The Hedge connect after every request in earlier logs is the hedge consuming the spare, so the keep-for-next-request path stays. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex-client -p nanocode-backend-codex` native and wasm32 (no warnings), `cargo clippy --no-deps` on both (only the existing `reconnect_delay` const-fn warning), `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 1000 5 --scenario runtime`: 1,000 passed, 0 failed.
- perf(python-capi): msgpack's packer and ujson's dumps cross into RustPython far less: PyType_IsSubtype answers from the tp_base chain, PyUnicode_AsEncodedString and PyUnicode_AsUTF8String build UTF-8 bytes in C, PyDict_Next walks the dict's own entries, and a dict crossing no longer runs the datetime checks first (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 bug-fix wave: regex, msgpack and ujson in python.wasm against Pyodide). Profiled natively with callgrind on a release build with line tables: PyType_IsSubtype was 32% of msgpack packing (520,000 calls in four packs of 5,000 records, about 380 instructions each, since both type objects crossed to RustPython, took a STATIC_TYPES lookup and a clone, then walked the MRO), because Cython's PyFloat_Check, PyDict_Check and the like call it for every value that is not exactly that type; ujson's dumps spent 53% in PyUnicode_AsEncodedString, which called `str.encode` through the codec registry for every key and string; PyDict_Next copied each dict's items into a per-dict snapshot map; and every dict that crossed to C ran the datetime type tests (four `_Py_datetime_type` lookups and subclass checks) before the dict branch. What: PyType_IsSubtype (types.rs) returns 1 for `object` and for any type on `a`'s tp_base chain, and 0 for a type without Py_TPFLAGS_HEAPTYPE (a static type has one base, and `c_type` builds its class from tp_base alone, so the VM answered the same); only heap types still go to RustPython's MRO. PyUnicode_AsEncodedString with a NULL or UTF-8 encoding name and PyUnicode_AsUTF8String make the bytes object in C (Kind::Pending, as PyBytes_FromStringAndSize does) from an ASCII str's own data or from the str's UTF-8 when it holds no surrogates, and otherwise call `encode` as before, so error handlers still apply; like CPython they no longer call a str subclass's `encode`. PyUnicode_AsUTF8AndSize returns an ASCII str's data before crossing it. PyDict_Next uses `PyDict::next_entry` with the position as the entry index (CPython's meaning: a value replaced during the walk is seen, a negative position ends it), and the SNAPSHOTS map and `forget_snapshots` go. bridge.rs: `proxy` tries dict and slice before the datetime layouts; `type_pointer` returns the static type of an exact str, int, float, dict, list, tuple or bytes without the C_TYPES lookup; `sweep` removes the swept proxies' map entries in one borrow. Bench (~/lanes/perf/bench.py and op.py, outside the repo): 5,000 records `{id, name, score, active, tags: [3 str], parent: None}` through msgpack.packb/unpackb and ujson.dumps/loads, and over 1 MiB of 8-word lines regex `\d+` sub, `\s+` split and `\w+` finditer with `m.group()`. Instructions per operation (perf stat -e instructions:u of `op.py <op> 10` less `op.py <op> 0`, divided by 10, native release, before/after): msgpack pack 175.2M/112.0M, unpack 181.0M/167.9M, ujson dumps 261.2M/102.6M, loads 190.6M/185.3M, regex sub 305.2M/298.2M, split 643.2M/626.7M, finditer 1687.8M/1666.8M; ablations: dict before datetime alone pack -6.6% and unpack -4.3%, builtin type pointer -1.5 to -2%, one-borrow sweep -0.5 to -0.9%, next_entry pack and dumps -3.5%. Native ms (best of 5 per run, 5 interleaved runs, medians, before/after): pack 14.74/9.79, unpack 21.08/20.58, dumps 31.79/8.60, loads 24.13/22.84, sub 32.94/31.50, split 77.81/75.42, finditer 197.55/196.57. python.wasm (nanocode-ts scripts/python.mjs build with NANOCODE_PYTHON_SOURCE, wasm-opt -Oz and bake as build.mjs does, run through the Bash API in Node 24, 7 interleaved runs, medians, before/after): pack 17.25/12.27, unpack 19.58/18.72, dumps 31.27/12.37, loads 22.05/20.66, sub 32.48/31.79, split 69.87/68.36, finditer 195.79/196.58 (Pyodide 314.0.7 on the earlier bench: pack 6.5, unpack 8.8, dumps 15.9, loads 12.6). Tried and dropped, no gain in instructions: immortal proxies for the empty tuple, empty str and RustPython's cached small ints (finditer -1%, unpack +0.3%), a lazy method name in `invoke` (with it, within 1%), an ASCII path in PyUnicode_FromKindAndData (ujson loads +2%). Left: unpack, loads and regex are bound by creating a RustPython object and its C proxy per value (map insert, queue, sweep) and by RustPython's own dict inserts and str creation, about 1,000 instructions per created str. Unchanged, before and after: msgpack 154 passed and 7 skipped, ujson 476 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed, regex 101/101 natively and in python.wasm; pyyaml's 2,609 and markupsafe's 79 (1 skipped) natively. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-python-capi -- -D warnings`, `cargo +1.97.1 check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python-capi --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (warnings only in rustpython-vm, as before), `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-python-cli`. Files: crates/core/python-capi/src/{api.rs,bridge.rs,types.rs}.
- fix(claude): a turn that fails or is cancelled reports the cost of the model calls it completed (2026-11-14). `emit_run_finished` took usage only from a completed turn's result, so the `run.failed` of a cancelled turn (an evaluation attempt stopped at its agent timeout, Esc in the TUI) or of a failed one carried `cost_usd: null`, `cost_status: other` and no `estimated_cost`, although each of its completed calls had reported its tokens in `model.call.completed`: a host that adds up the terminal events under-reported every attempt that ran out of time. Now `run` owns the turn's running `Usage`: `run_rounds` adds every response to it where it added to a local of its own (the value it also stores in the cursor, so a resumed turn starts from what the cursor kept), and `emit_run_finished` falls back to it when the result is an error. A turn that ends before its first response reports `other` and no cost as before, and a panicked turn has no usage at hand and is unchanged. Where a turn that failed is later resumed from its cursor, its last terminal event reports the usage of the whole turn, as it did, and the earlier `run.failed` now reports the part before it: a host that adds the two counts that part twice. Codex needs no change: its terminal event, whatever the outcome, is built from `RunStats`, to which every response adds (`emit_terminal` in model/run/turn.rs; read, not run). Checked with output/cancelled-cost (the facade's Claude agent on Haiku 5.5 against a local Messages endpoint that answers the first request with one exec call and a usage of 1,000 input and 100 output tokens and holds the second request open; the harness cancels the turn when model call 2 starts): before, `run.failed {status: cancelled, cost_usd: null, cost_status: other, estimated_cost: null}`; after, `{status: cancelled, cost_usd: 0.00015, cost_status: estimated_from_usage, estimated_cost: {input_usd: 0.0001, output_usd: 0.00005, usd: 0.00015}}`, the price of that one call. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, and `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -- -D warnings` on both targets report nothing. Run again on c97e1a49f, where a hedged call adds its duplicate's input to the call's estimated cost before `run_rounds` adds the response (1d4463636), so the fallback carries it too (read, not run: the harness does not hedge): the harness, moved from tokio to nanocode-executor, gives the same two payloads before and after, and the same commands report nothing; scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs stops on c97e1a49f itself, with and without this change, at `nanocode-backend-codex-client → nanocode-agent-core`, the dependency hedging added. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs.

- fix(claude, codex): a model call whose stream stalled is asked again once, and when the next attempt stalls too the call fails with an error that is not retryable, so a provider that has gone silent fails the turn after about 600 s instead of being asked up to 11 (Claude) or 35 (Codex) times and then re-driven by a durable host (2026-11-14). The idle bounds (300 s: the Codex WebSocket and HTTPS stream, the Claude client's `read_timeout` and, since the entry below, its host transport) turned a hang into a retryable failure, and the retry rules then treated a stall like any transport error. Claude's loop allows 11 attempts (3 for a call without tools): 55 minutes of silence. Codex allows 5 attempts, then, on a WebSocket, the HTTPS fallback with 5 more, then `STREAM_MAX_RETRIES` (5) reconnect rounds of 5: 35 attempts by reading, 30 without a WebSocket. And the failure that ends such a call is still retryable, so the Codex driver persists `fail_attempt` and Claude settles `FailAttempt`: the turn stays pending and a durable host drives it again. Measured before, natively on the parent commit with every request stalling: a Claude turn through the native client against a scripted TCP server, stalled mid-body or never answered, lost attempts at 300.1, 600.7 and 901.8 s, each `model.attempt.retrying` naming 11, and was in its fourth when the harness gave up at 1,000 s; the Codex service, on a WebSocket and on HTTPS through a host, lost attempts 1, 2 and 3 of 5 at 300.0, 601.0 and 903.1 s and was in its fourth at 1,000 s. And on wasm32 with only the retry-once half of this change: after the second stall at 602 s the nanocode-ts host drove the same turn again at once, a third request at 602.2 s for Codex, a `retry` answer that disposes the runtime for Claude. Now a stall is counted per model call. Codex: `ResponsesError::is_stall` is `ReceiveTimeout`, or a timed-out `HttpRequest` whose detail ends with `idle::STALLED` ("the stream stalled"), the words that only `stream_stalled` and the Chat Completions `stalled` write: the idle bound of the WebSocket and of the HTTPS stream natively and through a host, and a Chat Completions gateway's `stall_timeout`. The native layer also sets `timeout` for a connect that timed out and for a read the system timed out; those are not stalls, keep the usual attempts and stay retryable at the end; `ResponsesRetryPolicy::retry` lets the first one through to the usual retry (a new socket or request, full replay, 0.9 to 1.1 s later) and remembers it in `ResponsesAttempt::stalled`; at the second it returns no retry, before the HTTPS fallback and the reconnect rounds, and rewrites the failure (`ResponsesServiceError::stalled_again`): `ReceiveTimeout` becomes `Receive { reconnectable: false }`, `HttpRequest` keeps its detail with `retryable: false, timeout: false`, both ending ", twice in a row", so `retry_advice` is none and the driver persists `fail`. Claude: a stall is `HttpError::Transport { timeout: true, unsent: false }` (the native read timeout and the host bound; a connect timeout is unsent and keeps the usual attempts); the first is retried as before (0.5 to 0.625 s later), the second ends the loop and is rewritten the same way, so `BackendFailure::retryable` is false and the turn settles `Fail`. One retry because the retry is what a dead connection needs and it always opens a new one, while a second silence on a new connection says the provider is not answering this request, and each further attempt costs another 300 s in which nothing is shown; two bounds are 600 s, which is `retry::PATIENCE`, the time both backends already give a provider that answers 429, 502, 503, 504 or 529. Not retryable at the end because otherwise the bound is only moved up a level: a durable host has no count of its own for a turn it drives again. Rejected: upstream's stream retries (codex-cli asks 5 more times, 30 minutes), which suit a person watching "Reconnecting" and not a session under a caller's deadline; a budget of measured silence against `retry::PATIENCE`, which needs the length of each silence and neither `HttpError` nor `ResponsesError::HttpRequest` carries it, for the same result at the default bound; no retry at all, because the stall that started this (a WebSocket silent after model call 6, whose turn redid the call in 58 s once it was revived) is cured by one. Unchanged: a warm-up has one attempt of its own, so a stalled warm-up costs 300 s and the generation after it still has its two; a Claude request that declares server tools is not asked again after any uncertain failure, so its first stall ends the call, retryable, with the recovery notice, as before; `model.attempt.failed` of the second stalled Codex attempt still says `retryable: true`, since the service writes it before the policy decides, and the error of `run.failed` and of the turn is the rewritten one; every other transient failure keeps its attempts and stays retryable at the end. After, natively with every request stalling (output/idle-stall for the Codex service, output/claude-stall for a Claude turn): Codex WebSocket: attempt 1 failed at 300.1 s, attempt 2 at 601.1 s, the call failed with "failed to receive a Responses WebSocket frame: the Responses WebSocket sent no frame for 300 seconds, twice in a row; the stream stalled"; Codex HTTPS through a host, mid-body and before the head: failed at 600.9 s with "Responses HTTPS request failed: the Responses stream sent no data for 300 s; the stream stalled, twice in a row"; Claude, six cases (never answered, head only, mid-body; native client against a scripted TCP server and a scripted host transport): one `model.attempt.retrying` at 300.0 to 300.1 s, then `run.failed` at 600.6 to 600.7 s with "Messages transport: the Messages stream sent no data for 300 s; the stream stalled, twice in a row" through a host and "Messages transport: request or response body error: operation timed out, twice in a row" through the native client. With only the first request stalling all nine completed on the second attempt at 300.6 to 301.1 s. A timeout that is not the idle bound is not a stall: against a listener whose accept queue is full, so that each connect ends in the system's timeout, the native Codex client lost attempts 1, 2 and 3 at 136.6, 271.8 and 409.0 s (`https_timeout`) and began attempt 4 at 412.8 s, as c97e1a49f does (137.0, 272.2 and 409.4 s); with `timeout: true` alone as the test, an earlier state of this change, the call ended for good at the second, 270.7 s, with ", twice in a row". A Claude turn through the native client against the same listener (its connect timeout of 30 s, `unsent`) was at attempt 9 of 11 at 381.2 s, before and after. After, on wasm32 (nanocode-ts master beside the nanocode revision it pins, with the WebSocket idle timeout and these three entries applied; its host in Node, a scripted `dispatch` and socket, an in-memory SQLite store): every request stalling: Codex HTTPS mid-body 300.6 and 601.8 s, before the head 301.1 and 602.1 s, WebSocket 300.6 and 601.7 s, Claude never answered 300.6 and 601.2 s, head only 300.9 and 601.5 s, mid-body 300.7 and 601.4 s; in all six `drive` answered `finished` with the turn's status `failed` and the rewritten error at 601.3 to 602.2 s and no third request or socket followed; only the first stalling: all six completed at 301.3 to 302.1 s; the same twelve runs with the stall test narrowed to the idle bound's own words: failed at 600.9 to 601.9 s, completed at 301.0 to 301.9 s. Reported, not changed: nanocode-ts closes a host WebSocket after the milliseconds its egress names in `x-nanocode-stream-idle-ms`; the brain sees `Closed`, class `premature_close`, which is not a stall: on the released build-f3aa94f with 3,000 ms and every socket silent, five sockets were closed at 3.3, 7.5, 12.4, 19.2 and 30.6 s and the call then fell back to HTTPS, so a host that names a value at or below 300,000 gets the old five attempts instead of this rule. Run again natively on c97e1a49f, after nanocode's own executor replaced tokio (c2ee03965) and hedged requests arrived (1d4463636, off unless a host asks), with both harnesses moved to nanocode-executor. Before: the three Claude host cases and the Codex host head had not ended at 420 s; with every request stalling the native Claude client lost attempts at 300.2, 600.9 and 902.0 to 902.1 s of 11 and Codex, on the WebSocket and on HTTPS through a host, at 300.1 to 300.2, 601.1 to 601.3 and 903.3 to 903.5 s of 5, all still going at 1,000 s. With this entry and the two below: every request stalling failed after two attempts at 601.1 to 601.2 s (Codex, three transports) and 600.9 to 601.0 s (Claude, six cases) with the errors above, and only the first stalling completed at 301.0 to 301.2 s and 300.7 to 300.8 s. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-codex-client -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-codex`, natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, pass; `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-codex-client -p nanocode-backend-claude -- -D warnings` on both targets: one finding, the `reconnect_delay` const-fn lint in retry.rs that the WebSocket idle timeout entry already names, in code this change does not touch, and c97e1a49f stops at it the same way; `-D warnings` passes for the two Claude crates, and without it the three crates report nothing else. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs, crates/backends/codex/client/src/{tower/attempt.rs,tower/middleware/retry.rs,tower/service_error.rs,transport/chat.rs,transport/error.rs,transport/http.rs,transport/idle.rs}.

- fix(claude): a Messages response read through a host `HttpTransport`, which is every Claude request of a WebAssembly brain, fails with a retryable timeout when the host sends nothing for 300 s, before the head or between two body chunks, instead of holding the turn (2026-11-14). The native client has bounded both since "fix(claude): bound the Messages connection with a connect timeout and a stream idle timeout", through nanocode-http's `read_timeout`. A client over a host transport (`HttpClient::new` on wasm32, `ClaudeClient::with_transport` natively) had no counterpart: `transport::post_with` awaited `HttpTransport::post` bare, `stream_prepared`, `text` and `json` awaited each body chunk bare, and `MESSAGES_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT` did not exist on wasm32. Reproduced three ways, a host that never answers the request, one that answers the head and nothing else, and one that sends `message_start`, `content_block_start` and one `content_block_delta` and then goes silent: natively with output/claude-stall (a turn of a session built with `Nanocode::builder().claude(client)`, the client over a scripted `HttpTransport`) the turn had not ended when the harness gave up at 420 s in all three; on wasm32 (the released nanocode-ts build-f3aa94f, its host in Node driving a Claude session against a scripted `dispatch`) all three were still waiting at 330 s, in the two cases with a head with one more request at 300.1 s that is the prompt-cache keep-alive (`stream: false`, `max_tokens: 0`), not a retry. Now `MESSAGES_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (300 s) is defined on both targets and every post to a host transport runs under `nanocode_platform::timeout` (`transport::post_idle`); with an HTTP layer the bound sits in the innermost sender, so each of a layer's own round trips is bounded and the layer is not. The response it returns has its body wrapped (`HttpResponse::idle`): each chunk is awaited under one lazily reset timer per response, the shape of the Codex client's `IdleTimer` (the two client crates share no crate that has `select`, so the 20 lines are repeated in transport/host.rs), which also bounds `text` and `json` of a non-streaming or rejected response, the keep-alive request and the drain after `message_stop`. A lapse is `HttpError::Transport { retryable: true, timeout: true, unsent: false }` with the detail "the Messages stream sent no data for 300 s; the stream stalled", which `ClaudeError::is_transient` already retries and `retry_class` already names `transport_timeout`; dropping the pending post or the body is what tells the host to give the request up (nanocode-ts aborts its fetch or cancels the body reader). A client over nanocode-http is untouched: its `read_timeout`, which a caller of `messages_api` chooses, stays the only bound there, and a second timer would override a longer one. After, natively (with the entry above this one applied as well): in all three host cases `model.attempt.retrying` (`transport_timeout`, attempt 1, delay 0.585 s) at 300.0 to 300.1 s and the turn completed with the second answer at 300.6 to 300.7 s; the same three cases against a scripted TCP server through the native client, which this change does not touch, retried at 300.1 s and completed at 300.7 s, so the two transports now behave alike. After, on wasm32 (nanocode-ts master beside the nanocode revision it pins, with the WebSocket idle timeout and these three entries applied; the module built with `cargo build --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --profile wasm`): never answered: the request aborted at 301.1 s, the second request at 301.7 s, the turn completed at 301.8 s; head only: the body cancelled at 300.9 s, completed at 301.6 s; mid-body: cancelled at 300.6 s, completed at 301.3 s. Per request the host armed two 300,000 ms timers, one for the head, cancelled when it arrives, and one for the body, beside the keep-alive's own; none per chunk. The simulator's `--wire transport` builds its client the same way and now carries the bound too; its slowest head is 180 s and its largest chunk gap 500 ms (`SLOW_HEADERS_MS_MAX`, `CHUNK_GAP_MS_MAX`), so no seed reaches it; not rerun. What a second stall does is the entry above. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-codex-client` and `-p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-codex`, natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, pass. Files: crates/backends/claude/client/src/{lib.rs,transport.rs,transport/host.rs}.

- fix(codex): the 300 s idle bound also holds for an HTTPS Responses stream read through a host transport, as on wasm32, and for a Chat Completions gateway's head there (2026-11-14). Follow-up to "fix(codex): a Responses WebSocket that sends no frame for 300 s fails the attempt with a retryable `ResponsesError::ReceiveTimeout`" of the same date, which bounded both WebSockets and made `transport::idle::IdleTimer` real on wasm32; it left the HTTPS path with three bare waits. On wasm32 the SSE stream had no timer at all: `idle`, `idle_within`, `stream_stalled` and `SseStream`'s `IdleTimer` were native-only and the `SseBody::Host` arm awaited `body.next()` bare, so a host body that went silent held the turn for good; this is the stream of every session that pays by key or through a Responses gateway while its brain runs as WebAssembly. On both targets the head of a host `http` call (`ResponsesHttp::send_host`) was awaited bare, while the native client's head already ran under `idle()`. And `ChatGateway`'s `stall()` ignored its timeout on wasm32, which left a gateway's head and its compaction body unbounded there (its streamed body reads go through `IdleTimer`). Now the wasm32 `cfg`s around them are gone: the SSE stream holds its one lazily reset `IdleTimer` on both targets and every host body read goes through `idle_within`, so no timer is made per chunk; the host `http` call runs under `idle()`, one `nanocode_platform::timeout` per request as for the native head; and `stall()` is `nanocode_platform::timeout` on both targets (`stall_timeout`, `DEFAULT_STALL_TIMEOUT` unless the caller set another). A lapse is the error these paths already had natively, `ResponsesError::HttpRequest { retryable: true, timeout: true }` ("the Responses stream sent no data for 300 s; the stream stalled", retry advice `https_timeout`; the gateway's own wording under `stall()`): no new error or constant. The WebSocket code of that entry is untouched: checked against it, a server that keeps pinging while the response is silent does not move its deadline (the native pump answers pings without waking the reader, and a host connection yields only text, close or binary), and the warm-up wait is covered because `receive_warmup` reads through the same `next_text`. Checked natively with output/idle-stall (own workspace, path dependencies, no credential, no network), which builds the client's service the way a session does and prints its `model.*` events against a scripted `HostTransport`, the path wasm32 takes for HTTPS, whose first `http` call either (a) answers `response.created`, `response.output_item.added` and one `response.output_text.delta` and then never yields another chunk, or (b) never answers its head, and whose later calls answer completely. With this change and the two entries above it: (a) `model.attempt.failed` (receive, `https_timeout`) at 300.0 s, the stalled body dropped, `model.attempt.retrying` with a 0.93 s delay, the second call and the completed answer at 300.9 s; (b) failed (send, `https_timeout`) at 300.0 s, completed at 301.0 s. On the parent commit: (b) was still waiting, with no error and no retry, when the harness gave up at 420 s; (a) was already bounded natively at 300.0 s, its gap was wasm32 only.
