- deps(pymath): pymath's wasm32 math takes the 28 functions djs-libm already carries from djs-libm, and its own port of the libm crate keeps only copysign, erf and erfc, exp2, frexp, modf, nextafter, pow, remainder and remquo, 1,014 of its 3,136 lines (2026-11-14, cutting vendored code: DEPENDENCIES.md rank 2, two libm ports side by side). What: crates/patches/pymath/src/m_rust.rs, the `m` of every target but unix and windows, calls `djs_libm::` acos, acosh, asin, asinh, atan, atan2, atanh, cbrt, ceil, cos, cosh, exp, expm1, fabs, floor, fmod, hypot, ldexp, log, log10, log1p, log2, sin, sinh, sqrt, tan, tanh and trunc; m_libm loses those 28 files with expo2, k_cos, k_expo2, k_sin, k_tan, rem_pio2, rem_pio2_large and scalbn (36 files), and the kept erf, exp2 and pow take exp, fabs, scalbn and sqrt from djs-libm; pymath depends on djs-libm only under `cfg(not(any(unix, windows)))`, so Linux, macOS, Windows and every native build (which call the C library through m_sys) and their binaries are unchanged; pow stays pymath's because djs-libm's is musl's current pow and gives other bits. Checks: output/libm-equality includes master's m_libm and this one with djs-libm, and compares all 38 functions m_rust reaches (the 28 now from djs-libm, scalbn, which the kept exp2 and pow call, and the 9 kept, whose helpers now come from djs-libm) bit for bit on seeded doubles: uniform bit patterns, normals in 2^-65..2^65, 40 special values (zeros, infinities, NaNs, subnormals, MIN_POSITIVE, MAX, pi/2 multiples, the exp overflow and underflow edges) moved by up to 4 ulps, integers and half-integers, multiples of pi/2 up to 2^61, values next to 0 and +-1, subnormals, and every exponent; second arguments drawn the same way and ldexp and scalbn exponents across -2200..2200 and the i32 edges. Built for wasm32-unknown-unknown and run under Node 24: 33,554,432 cases per function, 1,275,068,416 in all, 0 differences in any bit. Built for x86_64: 134,217,728 cases per function, 5,100,273,664 in all, 0 differences except NaN sign bits (on 16,777,216 cases per function, 8,069,953 of sqrt's and 7,185,070 of acosh's give 0xfff8000000000000 for a negative argument where the old port gave 0x7ff8000000000000: djs-libm takes the SSE2 sqrt there, as libm does, and that path is never built for wasm32; Python's math raises ValueError for those arguments either way). `cargo check --locked` of pymath for wasm32-unknown-unknown, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, and of rustpython-stdlib for wasm32-unknown-unknown (only master's warnings: pymath's unused `libc` on wasm32, rustpython-ruff_python_ast's cfgs, rustpython-vm's two, nanocode-sys's windows `getsockopt`); `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` (only master's warnings: rustpython-ruff_python_ast's cfgs and the two unused workspace dependencies). nanocode-cli and nanocode-sim do not link pymath, so the release `nanocode` is unchanged.
- deps(rustls): the vendored rustls loses finite-field Diffie-Hellman: the FFDHE groups' parameters (msgs/ffdhe_groups.rs), the TLS 1.2 DHE key exchange on both sides and `KeyExchangeAlgorithm`, 761 of its 26,865 lines (2026-11-14, cutting vendored code: DEPENDENCIES.md rank 1). What: `Tls12CipherSuite` drops `kx`, `SupportedKxGroup` and `ActiveKeyExchange` drop `ffdhe_group`, `ActiveKeyExchange` drops `complete_for_tls_version` (its only job was stripping a DHE secret's leading zeros for TLS 1.2, so the PRF and HKDF call `complete`), `NamedGroup` drops `key_exchange_algorithm` and `InvalidMessage` the never-built `UnsupportedKeyExchangeAlgorithm`; ServerKeyExchange and ClientKeyExchange carry only ECDHE parameters (`ServerEcdhParams`, `ClientEcdhParams`, a trailing byte still `InvalidDhParams`); the server picks the first offered group it has and then a suite by signature and version, which is what the old selection did whenever the provider held no FFDHE group and no DHE suite; the client sends EC point formats whenever it has a group; the builder's suite-to-group check goes (with ECDHE only it could fail only with no groups, which `no kx groups configured` already refuses). nanocode-tls's provider loses its eight `ffdhe_group` impls (all `None`) and its six `kx: ECDHE` lines. The `NamedGroup` names FFDHE2048 to FFDHE8192 stay, so a client's offered FFDHE group still reads and prints as before. Wire: graviola offers no FFDHE group and nanocode-tls no DHE suite, so every connection nanocode makes or serves is unchanged; a peer offering FFDHE groups or DHE suites gets what a rustls without them gives it. output/rustls-equality (master's rustls beside this one, side by side, seeded) checks it three ways, each with 0 differences: all four OLD/NEW client/server pairings on 30,000 deterministic cases (828 MB of wire bytes per pairing) and 3,000 real-crypto cases; `offer`, where master's client also offers one or two FFDHE groups (FFDHE2048, FFDHE3072, fake key shares of 256 and 384 bytes, at seeded places among its groups, so TLS 1.3 sends FFDHE key shares and gets HelloRetryRequests) and, in half the seeds, TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 among its suites, against master's server as nanocode configures it and this server (100,000 deterministic cases, 2.81 GB, and 5,000 real-crypto cases); `serve`, where master's server holds those groups and suites, against master's client and this client (100,000 deterministic cases, 2.81 GB, and 5,000 real-crypto cases). The same offers against a master server that does hold FFDHE give other bytes in 3,145 of 10,000 cases (DHE negotiated, other HelloRetryRequests), so the offers reach the removed code. Checks: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` (only master's warnings: rustpython-ruff_python_ast's cfgs and the two unused workspace dependencies); `cargo check --locked` of rustls and nanocode-tls for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin (only master's nanocode-sys windows `getsockopt` warning), and of nanocode-tls for wasm32-unknown-unknown, where it does not link rustls (rustls alone for wasm32 fails on master's `UnixTime::now` in time_provider.rs, unchanged); nanocode-sim, which links rustls through nanocode-sandbox, built in release and `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 300 2` gives SWEEP passed=300 failed=0, panics=0. Release `nanocode`: 73,969,184 to 73,951,072 bytes stripped (17.7 KiB smaller), `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-cli` at master and at this commit.
- nanocode-sim's cells scenario checks `cell_result_kept`: a turn that resumes an External cell whose result save and finishing save both returned `Ok` must find the call's `JournalEntry::Result` in the recovered journal, and the `ack_buffered_result` mutation, which counts the result kept at its buffered save, is caught (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 durability track: DST lane). The turnlog sweep failures that the restart lane measured on 2ccfcecdb and 9640273ef (331 of 2,000 seeds with `--twice`, all `cell_rows`: an External turn wrote 4 rows, not 3, or 3 buffered, not 2) came from 97866818c. Bisect: the first 50 failing seeds of `--seeds 0..300` on 2ccfcecdb (51 of 300 failed), `git bisect start 9640273ef 3cae6d89d -- crates/runtime/agent crates/runtime/code-mode crates/core/turnlog bin/nanocode-sim`, each step a release build of nanocode-sim and the 50 seeds with `--scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice`: 9ef8adae5 bad (50 of 50 failed), 97866818c bad (50 of 50), 01afd5d90 good (0 of 50), bf35cf9b9 good (0 of 50), so 97866818c is the first bad commit. That commit is a durability fix that pays one row per External turn by design (its entry says so): `OneLogJournals::save` commits once an External result is buffered and the cell finishes or waits, so a restart replays the answer instead of the unknown outcome. The sim's expectation was stale, not the product, and 0dff6b832 already moved `Kind::rows` for External from 2 to 3 (plus the admission row), so master 37f0aeb00 passes every turnlog sweep (`--twice` 0..2000 2,000 of 2,000; `--snapshot-rows 4 --state-bytes 131072`, `--calm --row-limit 1024` and `--snapshot-ratio 1` 0..1000 1,000 of 1,000 each; `--long 100` 0..200 200 of 200). No check covered the result that row keeps: `cell_rows` counts rows on clean turns only, and a resumed cell that got the unknown outcome for an answered call counted as `cell_unknown`, not as a failure. Now `Cells::answer` records an External cell whose save with the `Result` settled, and a later finishing save that settles marks it kept. A crash clears the in-process half, as the product's `OneLog::answered` is lost with its process. `plan` fails the seed when a kept cell's journal has no `Result`. Checked by hand with a product mutation (the `owed` and `answered` terms removed from the commit condition in `OneLogJournals::save`, so the result stays buffered): 553 of 2,000 `--twice` seeds fail, 238 on `cell_result_kept` and 315 on `cell_rows`. `--mutation ack_buffered_result` is caught by 114 of 2,000 `--twice` seeds. With the check, on b605ff2bf: `--twice` 0..2000 2,000 of 2,000; `--snapshot-rows 4 --state-bytes 131072`, `--calm --row-limit 1024` and `--snapshot-ratio 1` 0..1000 1,000 of 1,000 each; `--long 100` 0..200 200 of 200; `--children remote` 0..2000 2,000 of 2,000 and `--children local` 0..1000 1,000 of 1,000. Commands: `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh A B 3 --scenario turns --policy turnlog ...` with the flags above, `--scenario runtime --children remote` 0..2000 and `--children local` 0..1000. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-sim -- -D warnings` (only the two existing alloc.rs lints), rustfmt --edition 2024 on the two files. Files: bin/nanocode-sim/src/cells.rs, bin/nanocode-sim/src/turns.rs.
- fix(python): rustpython-host_env's winsound declares MessageBeep in a block linked to user32, the DLL that exports it, so nanocode-python links for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc. MinGW adds user32 to every link, which hid the missing library on windows-gnu; MSVC's link.exe reported LNK2019 for MessageBeep on GitHub's windows-latest runner (2026-11-14). Beep stays in kernel32's default block. Checked: cargo build -p nanocode-python-cli for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc on windows-latest links, and its smokes pass on both Windows targets.
- fix(python): nanocode-python runs on Windows: an 8 MiB main-thread stack, the win32 code-page codec module and POSIX paths for the working directory (2026-11-14, Georgios: nanocode-python on Windows). What: bin/nanocode-python's build script links the executable with an 8 MiB main-thread stack on Windows (`/STACK` for MSVC, `-Wl,--stack` for GNU), the main thread's stack the same binary gets on Linux (glibc's default 8 MiB RLIMIT_STACK) and macOS, and what upstream RustPython links its Windows binary with; rustpython-pylib's Lib gets back encodings/_win_cp_codecs.py from CPython 3.14.0, which encodings imports on win32 during the interpreter's essential initialization (the import census that cut Lib ran on Unix); `serve` gives the interpreter the working directory as a POSIX path on Windows (`C:\x\y` is `/C:/x/y`, a UNC path keeps its leading `//`), `machine_path` maps `/C:/...` back to `C:/...`, and the script path's `absolute` takes `C:\x` or `C:/x` as absolute and `\` as a separator on Windows only. Why: windows-latest's gnu debug build stopped in essential initialization with "RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded while hashing". The stack bounds are right: under wine64, GetCurrentThreadStackLimits gives the main thread low 0x7ffffe100000 and high 0x7ffffe300000 (the 2 MiB mingw reserve; MSVC's default is 1 MiB) with a 20 KiB guarantee, and nanocode-sys's `current_thread_stack_remaining_bytes` and rustpython-vm's soft limit (low plus the guarantee plus twice STACK_MARGIN_BYTES, 256 KiB in debug) read them correctly; the debug frozen-importlib bootstrap reached 1.83 MiB below the top (sp 0x7ffffe12c556 against the soft limit 0x7ffffe145000), so 2 MiB does not hold it, and with the reserve patched to 8 MiB it passes. Past that it failed on the missing encodings._win_cp_codecs, then on "the working directory is not an absolute path" (`C:\...`). Under wine64, the gnu and msvc debug builds print 42 for `print(6 * 7)`, run json, re, hashlib, os and pathlib (cwd, listdir, write, read and remove a file), raise RecursionError for unbounded recursion at the default limit, at `sys.setrecursionlimit(1000000)` and for `json.loads("[" * 100000)` without crashing, refuse `import subprocess` with ImportError exactly as the Linux build does (the program has no processes to run), and open the script by `Z:\...`, `Z:/...`, `/Z:/...` and a relative `..\...` path; the Linux debug build gives the same output with its cwd unchanged. output/winpy-steps.yml has the windows-latest steps that check the stack reserve and run these smokes for msvc and gnu.
- fix(python-capi): the C extensions compile and link for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (2026-11-14, Georgios: nanocode-python on Windows). What: include/pyconfig.h defines MS_WINDOWS, NT_THREADS and on 64-bit MS_WIN64 for `_WIN32`, as CPython's PC/pyconfig.h does, and HAVE_UNISTD_H, HAVE_PTHREAD_H and _POSIX_THREADS only off it, so Python.h's existing `#ifndef MS_WINDOWS` guard leaves out <unistd.h>; yaml._yaml's defines add YAML_DECLARE_STATIC, libyaml's switch for a static build, since yaml.h otherwise declares its functions `__declspec(dllimport)` on `_WIN32` and clang refuses the definitions for MSVC ("dllimport cannot be applied to non-inline function definition"); the build script links oldnames for MSVC targets, the library cl names in every object it compiles (clang's GNU driver names none), which maps POSIX names such as `strdup` (libyaml) to the UCRT's `_strdup`. Why: windows-latest's msvc build of nanocode-python-cli failed with "'unistd.h' file not found" at Python.h:45, and past it with the dllimport errors and an undefined `strdup` at link. Every file under c/ and ext/ compiles with clang-22 for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (xwin 0.6.5 splat of the MSVC CRT and Windows SDK 10.0.22621 headers through INCLUDE), x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and wasm32-unknown-unknown; `cargo build --locked -p nanocode-python-cli --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` links with lld-link-22 against the xwin libraries, and that nanocode-python.exe runs under wine64 (see the next entry).
- fix(python): nanocode-python and nanocode-python-capi build for Windows (2026-11-14, Georgios: nanocode-cli on Windows). What: python-capi's build script compiles its C with `clang` (or NANOCODE_CC / CC_<target>) for every Windows target, MSVC included, which has no `cc`, and leaves out `-fPIC` there, which clang refuses for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc ("unsupported option '-fPIC'"); `nanocode_python::serve` builds on every non-wasm target, taking the arguments, working directory and environment as `into_encoded_bytes` (the same bytes as `into_vec` on Unix) and mapping a path back with `OsStr::from_bytes` on Unix and UTF-8 on Windows; bin/nanocode-python's `main` and dependencies cover every non-wasm target. Why: python-capi's build failed on Windows hosts (no `cc`) and with `-fPIC` for MSVC, and nanocode-python-cli had no `main` off Unix (E0601). `NANOCODE_CC=clang-22 cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python-cli -p nanocode-python-capi --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` passes (the C extension objects compile for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu), and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python-cli` passes on Linux. Not verified here: the MSVC C build, which needs the MSVC headers (output/wincli-probe.yml builds nanocode-python-cli on windows-latest for msvc and gnu); bin/nanocode still runs no python3 utility on Windows, since no Windows nanocode-python is released.
- deps(psh): psh-utils' SHA-1 and SHA-2 come from nanocode-digest, which gains SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256; MD5 stays in psh (2026-11-14, rank 2 of DEPENDENCIES.md: psh-utils carried a third copy of the SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 compressions beside nanocode-digest's and graviola's). What: `sum_hash::Digest` is an enum over nanocode-digest's `Sha1`, `Sha224`, `Sha256`, `Sha384`, `Sha512`, `Sha512_224` and `Sha512_256` and psh's MD5, whose block buffering and padding moved into its own `Md5` (nanocode-digest has no MD5). sha*sum, `shasum -a 512224`/`512256`, md5sum and git call the same API. `Sha512_224` and `Sha512_256` are SHA-512 started from FIPS 180-4's initial values (5.3.6.1, 5.3.6.2) and truncated to 28 and 32 bytes; psh's shasum needs both. Equal: output/psh-digest-equal (master's sum_hash.rs beside this change's) for all eight algorithms: every length 0 to 2048 one shot, with empty updates, a byte at a time, at every two-piece split up to 300 bytes and at 8 random splits, 543,936 checks; then seeds 1 to 200 by 20,000 cases of 0 to 150,000 bytes (random, or one repeated byte) in up to 12 random pieces, 4,000,000 cases; 12,547,136 checks (digest, one-shot digest, hex, tag and length), 0 differ. On this host (SHA-NI, no SHA-512 instructions) SHA-1 and SHA-256 run nanocode-sys' SHA-NI path in both and SHA-512 the portable one. psh-utils' tests: 459 passed before and after, the same 3 fail (corpora not in the tree). Size (measured on 1d4463636, before the rebase onto ff7edbdf4, which touches neither file): the release `nanocode` 74,175,440 to 74,034,064 bytes, .text 49,953,752 to 49,943,432; against master, both commits: 74,063,824 to 74,034,064 (-29,760), .text 49,965,064 to 49,943,432 (-21,632). Lines: -473, +205 (psh-utils -372, nanocode-digest +93). Packages unchanged (128); psh-utils gains the path dependency nanocode-digest, which the psh workspace's lock adds. Commands as the previous entry (run on this commit): `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` with only master's warnings, the wasm32 checks of nanocode-digest and psh-wasm, clippy of nanocode-digest and psh-utils (no new warnings: MD5 walks `as_chunks`), nanocode-sim sweep 0..300 passed 300. Upstream delta: psh Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, psh-utils Cargo.toml, src/sum_hash.rs.
- deps(psh): psh-utils inflates with nanocode-compression's inflate, its own 798-line inflate.rs goes, and nanocode-compression's fast decoder reports zlib's messages (2026-11-14, rank 1 of DEPENDENCIES.md: psh-utils carried a second inflate beside nanocode-compression's). What: `codec::Inflater` keeps psh's interface (`new(Format)`, `reset`, `inflate(input, InputEnd, &mut Vec, limit)` answering `Progress::Done { consumed }` or `NeedsInput`) over `nanocode_compression::inflate::Inflate` with window bits -15 (raw) or 15 (zlib). Each call grows the Vec to its capacity, never past the limit, and inflates into the spare room until the stream ends or the input runs out; at the limit it inflates into a one-byte probe, so a symbol that would be written fails as `Failure::OutputFull`, the stream's end still answers Done, and running out of input answers NeedsInput (More) or `Failure::Truncated` (Final); every other failure is `Failure::Invalid` with zlib's message. git's loose and packed objects, gzip, gunzip's partial output and unzip call it as before. The fast decoder (`inflate/fast.rs`) moved the inflater to Bad without a message, so the next step of the same call replaced it with "repeated call with bad state"; it now fails with "invalid literal/length code", "invalid distance code" or "invalid distance too far back", as the slow path and zlib do (PNG, HTTP, turnlog and RustPython's zlib get the right message; statuses and bytes are unchanged). Equal: output/psh-inflate-equal (its own workspace: master's inflate.rs and codec.rs beside this change's codec.rs), xorshift seeds 1 to 60 by 5,000 cases: raw and zlib streams from `miniz::compress_to_vec` levels 1 to 9, stored blocks, sync-flushed multi-block streams and random bytes behind fixed and dynamic block headers, half of them corrupted (bit flips, truncation, appended garbage, overwritten bytes), each inflated whole with Final, whole with More then Final, in up to 9 random pieces and, for compressed data, with a limit of its size, size plus or minus 1 or a random smaller one; and codec::inflate, gunzip of one and two members, gunzip_member and gunzip_partial on gzip files of the same data. 300,000 cases, 1,379,516 runs and 2,714,158 inflater calls, 0 where master inflates a stream and the new code gives other bytes or another consumed count, 0 where master rejects a stream the new code accepts other than through master's own OutputFull below. 1,270,109 runs are identical call by call. The other 109,407 differ only in which error or when: (1) master refuses a whole match that does not fit while zlib fills the output first, 90,070 runs, both OutputFull with master's output a prefix; (2) master fails OutputFull when the output is full and the input runs out mid-stream where zlib asks for more input, 9,451 runs, in 5,783 of which the next input finishes the stream (a valid pack object split at that point, which master's git reader refused); (3) zlib checks a code set when it builds the table (a missing end-of-block code, an incomplete code set, an all-zero code length code) where master decoded until it met an unassigned code, 9,881 runs, 9,738 with the same output and 143 where zlib stops earlier; 15 of them (3 codec::inflate calls) are streams master accepted whose only distance code is longer than one bit, which zlib, and so gzip, git and unzip, reject as "invalid distances set"; (4) zlib reads a zlib header's dictionary id before failing on FDICT, 5 runs. At the codec level 601,030 of 601,052 checks agree; gunzip_partial returns less in 17 (case 3) and never more, and one corrupted gzip file reports "format violated" instead of "crc error" (case 3). Speed: `psh-inflate-equal bench` (40 zlib streams, 1.1 MB, and 20,000 objects, 20 MB, reset between objects as git's reader does; 5 rounds on a loaded host) 0.7 ms against 0.6 to 0.7 ms and 166 to 195 ms against 168 to 224 ms. psh-utils' tests (`cargo test --locked -p psh-utils` in crates/patches/psh): 459 passed before and after; the same 3 fail before and after (the awk, jq and GNU grep corpora are not in the tree). Size (measured on 1d4463636, before the rebase onto ff7edbdf4, which touches neither file): the release `nanocode` (x86_64 Linux, stripped, `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-cli`) 74,063,824 to 74,175,440 bytes, .text 49,965,064 to 49,953,752; the growth is .rodata (+64,960), .rela.dyn (+34,848) and .data.rel.ro (+14,656), which the next commit, touching only psh-utils' digests, takes back to below master (.rodata 5,374,588 against 5,376,956), so it is where 16 codegen units without LTO place data, not new code. Lines: -810, +133. Packages unchanged (128). Commands: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` (only master's warnings: rustpython-ruff_python_ast's seven, its cfg warnings and two unused workspace dependencies); `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p nanocode-compression -p nanocode-digest -p nanocode-shell`; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression -p nanocode-digest --all-targets` (only nanocode-sys's three); in crates/patches/psh `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo check --locked -p psh-wasm -p psh-wasm-core --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p psh-utils --all-targets` (dump.rs's two, as on master); nanocode-compression is simulated, so `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-sim` and `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 300 2`: passed 300, failed 0, 0 panics (run on the two commits together). Upstream delta: psh-utils src/codec.rs, src/git/store.rs, src/lib.rs, src/inflate.rs deleted.
- feat(cli): nanocode starts on Windows with psh as the shell of its commands, served by its own executable as on macOS (2026-11-14, Georgios: nanocode-cli on Windows). What: nanocode-psh's `ARGUMENT`, `serve_if_requested`, `shell` and the `current_exe` form of `program` build on every non-wasm target, bin/nanocode takes nanocode-process, nanocode-psh, psh and psh-engine on every non-wasm target, and `run_with` makes psh the shell everywhere; only the in-process embedding (nanocode-psh-embedded, `embedded`) and the downloaded python3 utility (`SHELL_UTILITIES` is empty off Unix, since bin/nanocode/src/python.rs downloads a Unix nanocode-python) stay Unix-only. Why: on non-Unix hosts `run_with` printed "psh, the shell of its commands, is built for Unix hosts only" and exited 1 before any subcommand ran, though psh and psh-engine already build for Windows and nanocode-process spawns and stops commands there. Measured under Wine 9.0 (`/usr/lib/wine/wine64`, own WINEPREFIX) with `cargo build --locked -p nanocode-cli --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` (debug, 5 m 53 s, 202 MB): `nanocode.exe --version` prints `nanocode 0.7.0` (rc 0), `--help` prints the usage (rc 0), `sessions --all --home <empty temp dir>` and `sessions --home <same>` print nothing with rc 0 as on Linux, `psh-shell -c 'echo psh says $((6 * 7)); pwd'` prints `psh says 42` and `Z:/tmp`; the terminal interface in a pty (output/wincli/pty.py) enters the alternate screen in 1.1 to 2.6 s, draws typed `hello` in the composer, and exits with status 0 only on the third Ctrl+C (one and two presses leave it running: clear draft, arm, quit), so raw input reaches the app's own key handling. Not seen under Wine: Wine's tty console does not pass a pty resize on (0 bytes drawn after SIGWINCH) and renders its own screen, so the leaving `\x1b[?1049l` is not in its output; output/wincli-probe.yml runs the same smoke in a ConPTY on windows-latest.
- feat(tui): nanocode-tui runs on a Windows console: raw mode, size, resize and input go through console handles, and the VT parser reads the same bytes it reads from a Unix tty (2026-11-14, Georgios: nanocode-cli on Windows). What: nanocode-sys's `windows_sys` gains the console mode constants (ENABLE_ECHO_INPUT, ENABLE_LINE_INPUT, ENABLE_PROCESSED_INPUT, ENABLE_QUICK_EDIT_MODE, ENABLE_EXTENDED_FLAGS, ENABLE_WINDOW_INPUT, ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT, ENABLE_PROCESSED_OUTPUT, DISABLE_NEWLINE_AUTO_RETURN), WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT, `SetConsoleMode` and `ReadConsoleInputW`, each as windows-sys 0.61.2 defines it, and `console` gains safe wrappers: `console_mode`, `set_console_mode`, `window_size` (the visible window of `GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo`, not the buffer), `read_input` with `ConsoleInput` (a key-down UTF-16 unit, a buffer resize, or anything else), `pending_input`, and `Wakeup` (an auto-reset event) with `wait_input`, which waits on the console input handle and the wakeup with `WaitForMultipleObjects`. crates/tui/src/terminal/console.rs is the Windows `device`: `tty()` opens CONIN$, `enable_raw_mode` saves both modes and sets the input to VT input with window events and without echo, line input, processed input (so Ctrl+C arrives as 0x03, as with ISIG cleared on Unix) or quick edit, and CONOUT$ to VT processing without newline auto-return (OPOST's counterpart); `disable_raw_mode` restores both; `size` reads CONOUT$, else stdout. crates/tui/src/input/console.rs is the Windows `EventStream`: a reader on the executor's blocking pool (`spawn_blocking`) waits for console input, turns key-down units into UTF-8 (a surrogate pair split across reads is joined; a lone surrogate becomes U+FFFD), reports `Event::Resize` from WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT with the size read again, and tells the parser more bytes follow while records are pending; dropping the stream sets the wakeup so a reader parked in the wait returns instead of taking the next key. Why: the TUI imported `std::os::fd`, `nanocode_sys::unix` and `signal::unix` unconditionally, so nanocode-tui failed for every Windows target with 7 errors. Process Ctrl+C (`signal::ctrl_c`, the hand's `ctrl_c` arm in bin/nanocode) already goes through `signal::windows::ctrl_c`; in raw mode the TUI gets Ctrl+C as a key, as on Unix. Not covered: conhost sends WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE_EVENT only when the buffer changes, so a height-only window resize with scrollback is seen at the next drawn frame (each frame reads the size), as in crossterm. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-tui -p nanocode-psh -p nanocode-cli` passes for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, and with `--lib` for wasm32-unknown-unknown.
- perf(cli): `nanocode exec --continue` picks the newest session of the workspace through a new `StateStore::newest_summaries` instead of `list_page`, which decoded every cached session summary into a `StateSummary` only to sort them and keep one (2026-11-14). What: `SessionStore::newest_page(workspace, limit, keep)` hands the JSONL store the workspace and a `SummaryFilter` (the catalog's own workspace, auxiliary-state and `keep` checks on a decoded summary); `Sessions::newest_summaries` runs the same classification as `list_summaries` (directory scan, statx, `.summaries` refresh, members, copied stores, unknown states), reads only `scope` and `updated_at_ms` of each known summary (a borrowed `Head` that validates the same fields and types as `StateSummary` but skips strings as raw values instead of unescaping them), stable-sorts the candidates of this workspace newest first in listing order, and fully decodes only until `limit` of them pass the filter; unknown states are returned as before, so the catalog still reads and remembers them and merges them exactly as `list_page` did. The choice is the same as `list_page`'s: same scope test (`Path` equality), same tie order (listed before read, then listing order), and a candidate whose full decode fails becomes unknown as in `list_summaries`. Stores without the method (default `Ok(None)`) and non-UTF-8 workspaces fall back to `list_page`. `listed` also computes each file's `dev:ino` identity once instead of formatting it again in `list_summaries`. Checked on copies of a 14,600-session store (~/wave/stores/nc) against bin-master step by step with a fake model: after a new session, after another process appended to an older session (with and without restoring `.summaries` so the append is unknown), after a newer session in another workspace, after a process killed mid-turn, and with subagent members newer than their root, both builds continued the same session at every step. Measured with `perf stat -e instructions:u,instructions:k,page-faults,task-clock` on `nanocode exec --continue` (taskset -c 16-19, bin-master and this build interleaved run by run on their own copy of the store, 24 rounds after a warm-up, BOLT shipped builds), median [p25, p75]: instructions:u 554.4M [547.7M, 563.2M] -> 475.7M [473.1M, 484.5M], instructions:k 235.6M [235.0M, 237.9M] -> 209.0M [207.4M, 209.4M], page faults 16,357 -> 11,661, task-clock 94.7 ms -> 84.9 ms, wall 97.6 ms -> 86.1 ms; an earlier 20-round run under heavier load gave wall 147.8 -> 123.8 ms. What remains is the classification itself (parsing the 11 MB `.summaries` into owned entries, readdir and statx of every session file), which `exec --resume <id>` (60M/98M instructions) does not pay. `cargo check --locked --lib` passes for nanocode-durability-core, nanocode-durability and nanocode-store-jsonl on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and wasm32-unknown-unknown, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` passes.
- deps(rustls): the vendored rustls loses QUIC, Encrypted Client Hello and HPKE, the unbuffered API, kernel TLS connections and secret extraction, the session ticketer, the blocking `Stream`/`StreamOwned` wrappers, the server `Acceptor`, FIPS reporting and the AEAD `extract_keys` hook, 6,204 of its 33,069 lines (2026-11-14, cutting vendored code: DEPENDENCIES.md rank 3, public API no nanocode crate or crates/patches user reaches). What: quic.rs, client/ech.rs, crypto/hpke.rs, conn/unbuffered.rs, conn/kernel.rs, ticketer.rs and stream.rs go; `CommonState` drops its QUIC state, `Protocol`, `enable_secret_extraction` and `fips`; `ClientConfig`/`ServerConfig` drop `enable_secret_extraction`, the ECH mode and `fips()` (`require_ems` defaults to false, which `provider.fips()` always gave with nanocode-tls's graviola provider); `Tls13CipherSuite` drops `quic`, `Tls12AeadAlgorithm`/`Tls13AeadAlgorithm` drop `extract_keys` and every provider trait its `fips()`, so nanocode-tls's provider loses its four `extract_keys` impls, `quic: None` and the X25519MLKEM768 `fips()`; the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 client and server state machines no longer thread `KernelState`, `ExpectQuicTraffic` or ECH state, and the QUIC transport-parameter extensions and the server's ECH acknowledgement leave `ClientExtensions`/`ServerExtensions` (an unsolicited one is now an unknown extension, which the client rejects with the same unsupported_extension alert as before; only a malformed body of one, which used to be a decode_error, now gets that alert too). Kept because they are reached or change the wire: TLS 1.2 on both sides (the egress proxy and the MPP proxy build `ServerConfig` with `with_safe_default_protocol_versions`, so TLS 1.2 clients reach them), the server's stateful TLS 1.3 tickets and session cache, X25519MLKEM768, the server's parsing of a client's ECH and ECH outer-extensions extensions (a malformed one stays a decode_error), and the HelloRetryRequest ECH check (an HRR naming ECH stays an unsupported_extension alert). Checks: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` (only master's rustpython-ruff_python_ast cfg warnings and the two unused workspace dependencies), and `cargo check --locked` of rustls and nanocode-tls for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-apple-darwin (with rustls-platform-verifier); rustls for wasm32 fails on master's `UnixTime::now` in time_provider.rs, unchanged here. output/rustls-equality runs master's rustls and this one side by side in all four client/server pairings: 30,000 seeded deterministic cases (seeded random, fixed time, fake key shares of the real lengths, real AEADs, HKDF and PRF; TLS 1.2 and 1.3, HRR, ALPN, SNI, fragment sizes, key updates, close_notify, then a resumed second connection: 7,557 TLS 1.2 and 13,550 TLS 1.3 full handshakes, 6,031 TLS 1.2 and 9,749 TLS 1.3 resumptions) compare 828 MB of wire bytes per pairing with 0 differences, and 3,000 real-crypto cases (graviola key exchange and fresh P-256 keys) agree on plaintext, parameters and errors with 0 differences; a ticket lifetime changed in a copy of the old crate was caught on the first differing record. output/live-get, the blocking nanocode-http client over the trimmed stack: https://api.anthropic.com 404, https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages 405, https://chatgpt.com 200. `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-cli` (CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2): `nanocode` 74,065,296 to 73,845,072 bytes (-215 KiB). Packages unchanged.
- perf(cli): the BOLT layout puts the one-shot prompt's functions in their own contiguous run after the terminal interface's startup functions, and the startup training also starts the terminal interface with `--ephemeral` (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: startup and exec RSS under 12 MB). scripts/train-cli.py gains a `oneshot` mode (one `exec --ephemeral` prompt against its fixture), build-cli.sh keeps its profiles in `oneshot/` beside `startup/` and merges both into the profile as before, and order-cli.py now takes the two directories and orders functions run only at startup, then those both run, then those only the one-shot ran, then the rest, each group in cdsort order. Why: file pages are most of both processes' RSS, and the kernel maps them in 64 KiB fault-around windows, so RSS is about 64 KiB per distinct window touched. `perf record -e page-faults -d` of master under bench/cli's netguard showed the one-shot touching 25 windows of the startup prefix, 27 more scattered over the rest of the 4.3 MB hot text (exec functions were in the profile but not in the startup set, so cdsort spread them) and 41 in .text.cold; and the terminal interface touching hot functions the startup training never ran because the bench passes `--ephemeral` (`MemoryStore::new`, `session_gateway`, `drive_grouped<MemoryStore>`). The training itself varies from build to build (four master trainings of the same pre-BOLT binary: first-frame RSS 11.79 to 12.52 MB, one-shot peak 13.38 to 13.75 MB), so the change was measured over several trainings: the pre-BOLT dist binary of master 37f0aeb00 laid out by build-cli.sh's BOLT steps three times with master's scripts and three times with these, plus bin-master, bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc --rounds=1` under tools/netguard.sh, pinned to 4 CPUs, 20 interleaved rounds per binary (dev-georgios, load about 60): one-shot peak RSS medians 13.38, 13.75, 13.38, 13.75 MB with master's layout against 12.50, 12.25, 12.75 MB; RSS one second after the first frame 11.79, 12.21, 12.08, 12.52 against 11.48, 11.50, 12.23 MB; one-shot CPU 7.31, 7.49, 7.15, 7.06 against 7.16, 7.01, 7.06 ms; first frame and its CPU unchanged within noise. `perf stat` of 20 interleaved one-shot runs: user instructions 8.52M for all, kernel 9.72M and 9.55M against 9.46M and 9.41M, page faults 752 and 748 against 740 and 729, task clock 5.98 and 5.84 against 5.93 and 5.74 ms. The shipped pipeline (scripts/build-cli.sh at this commit, BOLT 21) against bin-master, 20 interleaved rounds: one-shot peak RSS 13.75 [13.25-13.75] to 12.75 [12.50-13.00] MB, one-shot CPU 6.76 to 6.56 ms, first-frame RSS 11.95 to 12.03 MB (inside the training spread above), first frame 17.3 to 16.1 ms under load. Rejected in the same investigation: starting the Tempo paying proxy lazily in the terminal interface too (pre-BOLT A/B, 20 rounds: anonymous memory 1.99 to 1.92 MB, TUI CPU 10.4 to 9.0 ms, but no RSS change measurable against layout noise); the remaining one-shot gap is the bench's offline Tempo-tool failure path (19 of its 41 cold windows are DNS and MCP error code a networked training never runs) and rodata, where 48 touched windows (3.1 MB) fall on anonymous merged constants the linker places.
- perf(durability): the shared store's thread is started from the current executor when there is one, instead of on the thread that first spawns a driver (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: first frame <= 1.3 ms). The terminal interface's `MemoryStore::new` (and `SharedStore::new` around it) run in `Host::build` on the main thread before the first frame, and `spawn_driver`'s first call built the store runtime and spawned nanocode-durability-store there: uprobes put 65 us of the main thread in that thread spawn (the runtime build itself 4 us). `spawn_driver` still builds the runtime and spawns the driver onto its handle at once (the driver waits in the runtime's queue); the thread that runs it is spawned by a task on `nanocode_executor::Handle::try_current()`, on its worker for the TUI and `nc exec`, or in place when no runtime is current. If that thread cannot be spawned, the runtime is dropped with the closure, which cancels the queued drivers, so requests fail with "shared durability store stopped" as they did when a driver stopped. The main thread now creates the worker and, in 9 of 10 runs, the reactor's fallback thread (4 of 10 before: it registers stdin while the worker is busy) before the first frame. Measured as in the previous entry, against the previous change (same 30 interleaved rounds): main-thread task-clock to the first frame 1.355 [1.308, 1.425] to 1.325 [1.262, 1.417] ms, kernel instructions 3.241M to 3.233M; bpftrace main-thread on-CPU time 1,406 [1,323, 1,489] to 1,342 [1,311, 1,393] us, threads created before the first frame 3 to 2. Both changes against master: task-clock 1.495 to 1.325 ms (-11.4%), on-CPU 1,636 to 1,342 us (-18.0%). bench/cli suite (as above): first_frame_ms 16.8 (load-bound), RSS 1 s after the first frame 15.5 MB against 16.7 on master, CPU 26.2 ms; one-shot CPU 11.0 ms, peak RSS 13.75 MB, no errors. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-durability --no-deps -- -D warnings`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability` native and wasm32. Files: crates/runtime/durability/src/shared_store.rs.
- perf(cli): the terminal interface binds its reload socket after its first frame, writes a newly generated install_id after its first frame, and reads the window size from stdout before opening /dev/tty (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: first frame <= 1.3 ms). On the main thread before the first frame, `reload::Instance::start` made a mkdir (EEXIST), two statx, an unlink, a socket, a bind that creates the socket's inode, an ioctl and an epoll_ctl, and on a fresh home (every bench run) `install_id` made a mkdir, two opens, a write and a close; bpftrace timed the main thread's syscalls before the first frame at about 680 us per run on dev-georgios, mkdir alone 34 us a call. The event loop now starts the reload `Instance` right after it sets `FIRST_FRAME` (it is an `Option` the tail of `app::run` closes when present; a reload needs it and can only be asked for after the first frame); `install_id` still reads an existing id in place, and when it generates one it keeps it in memory and, for the TUI (`!config.headless`), saves it from a task that waits for `FIRST_FRAME` and writes on the blocking pool, while `nc exec` writes it in place as before; `terminal::device::size` asks stdout for the window size first, the terminal it draws on, and opens /dev/tty only when stdout is not a terminal. Measured with scripts/build-cli.sh builds (dist, BOLT 21) of 37f0aeb00 with and without this, pinned to 4 CPUs, interleaved, at load 45 to 60: main-thread counters from exec to the first frame (`perf stat --no-inherit`, the process killed when "Ask anything" appears, 30 rounds each, medians [p25, p75]) task-clock 1.495 [1.470, 1.548] to 1.355 [1.308, 1.425] ms, kernel instructions 3.451M to 3.241M, user instructions 1.122M to 1.119M, page faults 262 both; bpftrace (30 rounds) main-thread on-CPU time from exec to the first frame's write 1,636 [1,578, 1,757] to 1,406 [1,323, 1,489] us, exec to that write 2,173 to 1,509 us. bench/cli suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc, 12 alternating runs of 2 rounds each: first_frame_ms 16.4 and 16.7 (the loaded machine's scheduling decides wall time), RSS 1 s after the first frame 16.7 to 16.2 MB, CPU 28.6 to 26.4 ms; one-shot CPU 10.7 and 10.4 ms, peak RSS 13.6 and 14.0 MB, no errors. Checked: with and without --ephemeral the socket exists 2 s into the TUI and is gone after exit, install_id is written, and the screen shows no error; `nc exec` writes install_id. nanocode-ts does not run this code. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-tui --no-deps -- -D warnings`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tui` native and wasm32. Files: bin/nanocode/src/app.rs, bin/nanocode/src/host.rs, crates/tui/src/terminal/device.rs.
- perf(turnlog): the fold drops events once their row is committed, and `TurnLog::history` reads the unsealed segment from its rows (2026-11-14). The fold kept every committed event since the last boundary or snapshot row, up to the size of the state, only to answer history reads of the newest events; in a nanocode-ts parent whose children run in the same object, these are the children's forwarded events (an `input.accepted` carries the child's whole prompt), about 9 KB per child. `Lease::commit` (after its row is stored) and `TurnLog::open` (after each row) call `Fold::release`, which keeps only the first and last seq of the committed events since `segment_row` (`Fold::unsealed`). `history` scans that segment's rows `[segment_row, next)` as it scans a sealed one, then the events not yet committed. `hot_bytes` and the boundary rule are unchanged, so such a read decodes at most about the state's size, the bound that applied to memory before. `Fold::events` now holds only events not yet committed. `OneLog::import_events` compared an import against `lease.fold().events()`, the committed events of the unsealed segment, so the new `Lease::held(after, take)` reads those events from the same rows under the lease (one `scan` shared with `history`), followed by the events not yet committed. output/heldcheck (the 1,000-child log reopened with `snapshot_rows(Some(8))`, 400 commits of 1 to 3 events, a reopen every 37 commits, 6 `after` values per commit) returns the same 25,676 events with the same digest from `Lease::held` as from `Fold::events` before this change. output/hotcheck on the same 1,000-child log, 3 interleaved rounds: the fold held after open fell from 35,137,018 to 24,652,119 bytes (-30%) and the open peak from 37,921,922 to 28,079,466; `history(0)` returns the same 13,041 events with the same digest. The cost: a history read of the newest events now decodes the unsealed segment (132-202 ms for the last 20 events of this log, 0.0 ms before; 164-199 ms against 14-32 ms for all events). nanocode-ts reads the log only when its EventHub misses (a watcher behind, a client after a restart). Hill-climb (durable-cloudflare scripts/hillclimb.mjs on local workerd, in-object children, `--batch 100 --rate 200`, nanocode-ts bc9a923, bundles built on 3cae6d89d (before 0dff6b832, which nanocode-ts bc9a923 cannot build against) with and without the three turnlog commits, 2026-11-14, one run each): at `--agents 10000` the parent's peak wasm memory fell from 1,244.2 MB (124,420 bytes per child) to 585.4 MB (58,537 bytes per child, -53%), saturation rose from 0.126 to 0.176 and wall time fell from 810.7 to 582.5 s, workerd RSS from 2,308 to 1,549 MB, with rows written 1.11 per child in both and store bytes 17,084 against 18,095 per child; at `--agents 2000` the peak fell from 375.5 MB (187,728 bytes per child) to 123.3 MB (61,669 bytes per child, -67%), saturation 0.506 against 0.446 (earlier runs of one build ranged 0.445-0.473), rows 1.08 against 1.07 per child. The crash gate (`--agents 2000 --scenarios spawn,turn,done,twice`) passes on the change with 0 lost and 0 repeated children in every scenario (restart ready 1,639 ms, first model call 3,302 ms, list 1,724 ms). At `--agents 10000 --scenarios turn` (kill mid-turn with about 5,000 children done and 5,000 in flight, then restart) both pass with 0 lost and 0 repeated children; the turn scenario's peak wasm memory was 1,919 MB on the base and 1,336 MB on the change; restart ready 2,103 against 1,669 ms, list 13,392 against 7,939 ms, first model call 15,312 against 9,472 ms, but these restart times follow the shared host's load (load average 8 to 14 in the base run, 7 to 10 in the change run; an earlier change run under heavier load measured 2,075 / 13,082 / 15,162 ms), so they show no regression rather than a gain. The Lease::held part of this commit came after these bundles were built; output/heldcheck covers it. Checks: clippy and the wasm32 check as above, also for `nanocode-agent`; nanocode-sim turns turnlog sweeps all pass with no panics: `--twice` 0..2000, `--twice --snapshot-rows 4 --state-bytes 131072` 0..1000, `--calm --row-limit 1024` 0..1000, `--twice --snapshot-ratio 1` 0..1000, `--long 100` 0..200; `--mutation seal_skipped --without restart` is still caught (107 of 200 seeds fail).
- perf(turnlog): `TurnLog::open` and `TurnLog::history` decode and fold one logical row at a time (2026-11-14). `rows()` copied every stored body into a list and inflated all of them before the caller folded the first row, so a restart held the loaded bodies, their copies, the whole plain log and the fold at once. `each_row` consumes the loaded rows, joins one logical row's parts, inflates it and passes it on; `open` folds it and drops its plain text, and `history` stops at the first event the page refuses. `rows()` keeps its signature. `open` finds the extensible tail row of 0dff6b832 inside the same pass (the last stored row, when it starts a logical row without a `Recovery` record) instead of decoding every row first. `open` finds the last snapshot's parts before the fold, so `Previous` is computed once. output/hotcheck on the same 1,000-child log, 3 interleaved rounds against the previous commit: the peak of `TurnLog::open` fell from 63,829,734 to 37,921,922 bytes (-41%) and the fold it returns is unchanged (35,137,018 bytes held); open takes 202-241 ms against 190-220 ms. The wasm hill-climb of the three turnlog commits of 2026-11-14 together is in the entry above on events leaving the fold. Checks: clippy and the wasm32 check as above; `nanocode-sim --scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` seeds 0..2000, and seeds 0..1000 with `--snapshot-rows 4 --state-bytes 131072`, all pass with no panics.
- perf(turnlog): `Lease::commit` packs and measures a snapshot from `Fold::snapshot_records`, one record at a time, instead of cloning the fold into a `Vec<Record>` and encoding it into one string (2026-11-14, Georgios: at most 2 KB of parent memory per finished child). Every snapshot check built the whole snapshot body in memory, and the hot-event check (`measured`) did the same only to read its length, so the peak of linear memory was about three times the fold. `codec::Packer` compresses the stream as records arrive and keeps only the last window for the history; `measured` counts bytes without keeping them. `Fold::snapshot` keeps its signature and output. Measured natively with output/hotcheck (a counting global allocator around `TurnLog::open` on a `MemoryLog` holding the 1,022 rows of a 1,000-child nanocode-ts parent from the hill-climb, then `snapshot_rows(Some(1))`, one pushed event and one commit), 3 interleaved rounds against 0dff6b832, identical every round: the snapshot commit's peak fell from 75,455,674 to 10,518,711 bytes (-86%); the snapshot is 3,306,877 bytes against 3,285,891 (+0.6%: the stream is deflated in chunks with NoFlush); commit time 216-255 ms against 264-281 ms on a shared host. The wasm hill-climb of the three turnlog commits of 2026-11-14 together is in the entry above on events leaving the fold. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-turnlog -- -D warnings`, `cargo +1.97.1 check --locked -p nanocode-turnlog --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `nanocode-sim --scenario turns --policy turnlog` sweeps (below).
- feat: hedged first-byte model requests on the Responses and Messages routes (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 latency gate, decided by Georgios: provider-side slow sessions set nanocode's p99 on GPT turns 2-3 and DeepSeek). `nanocode_agent_core::hedge::Hedging` keeps, per model, a rolling window of recent requests' first-byte times and hedge flags in an `Atom`. `Hedging::race` waits for the primary's first byte until `max(policy floor, p90 of the window)`, then dispatches one duplicate and keeps whichever produces its first byte first, dropping the other (its connection closes, so the provider stops it). A hedge is admitted only while the window's hedges, counting it, stay at or under the cap's share of its requests, rounded up (so a short CLI process can hedge its first slow request). Policy comes from the host: `HedgePolicy::DEFAULT` is floor 1.5 s, p90, cap 10%, window 100 requests, and the CLI takes `--hedge-floor-ms`, `--hedge-cap-percent` (0 sends none) and `--hedge-window` (`NANOCODE_HEDGE_*`). Builders without a `Hedging` (`ClaudeBuilder::hedging`, `OpenAiBuilder::hedging`) never hedge, so library hosts such as nanocode-ts opt in. First byte means: on Messages, the response headers (Anthropic sends them with the first token: headers, `message_start` and the first delta arrived within 2 ms of each other in 5 of 5 live haiku requests from the hosted Hand); on Responses, the first event other than `response.created`, `response.in_progress` and `codex.*`, which `stream::first_output` buffers and `stream::Primed` replays into the unchanged receive loop, so nothing is emitted before the winner is known and no output is duplicated. On the Responses WebSocket the hedge opens its own connection (`ConnectionPurpose::Hedge`) and sends the request as a full replay. If it wins, `ResponsesService::install` makes it the session's socket (next generation) and drops the old one, so the next request continues from the winner's response id on the winner's connection. Messages thread turns and parked subagent calls do not hedge. Each hedge is reported: `model.call.completed` carries `hedge` (`dispatched` with `deadline_ns`, `winner`, `hedge_first_byte_ns`, or `capped`), the attempt span records `hedge.*`, and the duplicate's input (the winner's input tokens, cached and uncached, no output) is added to the call's estimated cost (Claude) and to the run's usage and cost (Codex). Checked with `output/hedge-harness` (a node mock of Messages SSE, Responses SSE and the Responses WebSocket, floor 400 ms): with the primary's first byte delayed 3 s, each route sent exactly one hedge 402-404 ms after the primary, rendered the hedge's reply (turn 414/418/414 ms instead of 3 s) and closed the primary within 2 ms of the hedge's first byte; with the primary at 700 ms and the hedge at 3 s, the primary's reply rendered at 709-714 ms and the hedge closed; the turn's estimated cost was $0.000205 against $0.000105 unhedged (1,000 input tokens counted twice); on the WebSocket the turn after a hedge win sent `previous_response_id` of the winner on the hedge's connection with one input item. `Hedging::race` over 60 requests that all miss a 50 ms deadline (quantile 0) dispatched 6 hedges and capped 54, ceil(10% x 60) = 6, and cancelled the 6 losing primaries; with one request in three slow at p90 the deadline rose to the slow time after one hedge and one capped request. `cargo check` native and wasm32 for nanocode-agent-core, the Codex client and both backends, and `cargo check -p nanocode-cli`. Live, claude-haiku-5-5 from the hosted Hand, 30 sessions of 3 turns per lane, interleaved, p50 / p99 ms for turns 1, 2 and 3 (SLA.md): hedging 751/1,775, 629/1,484, 633/1,295; the same build with cap 0 859/1,917, 705/1,361, 679/1,073; Claude Code 1,724/3,281, 1,035/1,819, 1,021/2,131. Only 2 of 90 cap-0 samples passed the 1.5 s floor, so haiku's tail is not a hedging case and the p99 deltas between the nanocode lanes are single samples.

- fix(executor): `JoinSet::poll_join_next` returns Pending and wakes its own task when a member's JoinHandle is pending because the task's cooperative budget is spent, instead of looping on that member forever (2026-11-14, Windows runtime probe under Wine 9.0, reproduced on Linux). A JoinHandle with no budget left wakes its waker and returns Pending (`coop::poll_budget`); in a JoinSet that waker pushes the member back onto the ready queue, and `poll_join_next_with_id`'s loop popped it again in the same poll, so the joining task spun at 100% CPU and never yielded to let the budget refill, as tokio's JoinSet avoids by yielding on a pending member. Found as executor.timer_storm (2000 tasks each sleeping `index % 50` ms, joined through one JoinSet) not finishing within 60 s in 1 of 4 full Wine runs and 2 of 15 isolated ones; gdb on a hung Linux process showed the block_on thread running in `Shared::pop` under `poll_join_next_with_id` and the worker idle in `epoll_wait`. Measured with output/timer-storm (release, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, one runtime reused per round unless `fresh`): before, `300 2 shared` hung after 30 rounds, `300 2 fresh` after 8, `300 1 shared` after 86 and `300 4 shared` after 7; after, 1000 rounds each of `2 shared`, `1 shared` and `4 shared` and 300 of `2 fresh` finish, and the Wine check passes 20 of 20. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-executor` passes for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-pc-windows-gnu.
- feat(executor): `signal::ctrl_c` resolves on Windows, and `signal::windows::ctrl_c` gives a `CtrlC` listener with `recv` and `poll_recv`, as `signal::unix::signal` does on Unix (2026-11-14, Windows runtime probe under Wine 9.0). What: nanocode-sys gains `console` (Windows only): `listen_interrupts` installs one `SetConsoleCtrlHandler` routine for the process, which counts each CTRL_C_EVENT in an atomic, calls the notify function the executor registered through an `AtomicStatic`, and returns TRUE; it returns FALSE for every other event (Ctrl-Break, close, logoff, shutdown), so Windows' default handling of those stays. The executor keeps a `Shared` list of weak listeners, wakes them from that routine, and a listener resolves once the count passes the value it saw when it was made, so a Ctrl-C from before `ctrl_c()` was called is not delivered to it. Before, `ctrl_c()` on Windows was `std::future::pending`, so bin/nanocode's `ctrl_c` arm (src/lib.rs) and tool-runtime's attachment runner never ran and Ctrl-C ended the process through the default handler. Measured with output/windows-runtime (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, `wine64`): executor.ctrl_c_delivery starts a child on its own console (CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE) that spawns `signal::ctrl_c()` and sends itself `GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent(CTRL_C_EVENT, 0)` 150 ms later; before, the default handler ended the child (exit 0 under Wine) and the check failed; after, `ctrl_c()` resolves and the child exits with its own success code, and executor.ctrl_c_registration still sees `ctrl_c()` stay pending without an interrupt. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-executor -p nanocode-sys` passes for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-gnu and wasm32-unknown-unknown.
- fix(sys): `current_thread_stack_remaining_bytes` reads the thread's stack bounds on Windows from `GetCurrentThreadStackLimits`, as it does from pthread on Linux, Android and Apple (2026-11-14, Windows runtime probe under Wine 9.0). Before, Windows fell into the `None` fallback, so the vendored ruff_python_parser's `caller_recursion_depth_max` never parsed in place there and every Python parse was handed to its `python-parser` worker thread and back. Measured with output/windows-runtime (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, `wine64`): before, win32.threads failed with "remaining None"; after, a 2048 KiB thread reports 2,094,151 bytes left inside its own `GetCurrentThreadStackLimits` range and the check passes. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-sys` passes for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-gnu and wasm32-unknown-unknown.
- fix(executor): on Windows a child's stdin, stdout and stderr do their reads and writes on the blocking pool through `fs::Blocking`, as `File` and the process's own stdio already do, instead of calling the pipe's blocking `read` and `write` inside `poll_read` and `poll_write` (2026-11-14, Windows runtime probe under Wine 9.0). Windows' anonymous pipes have no readiness the reactor can wait on, and the old code blocked the worker thread polling the pipe: a silent child stalled every other task on that worker, and `wait_with_output` deadlocked once a child filled the pipe it was not reading, because its `read_to_end` of stdout blocked in one poll while the child blocked writing stderr. Measured with output/windows-runtime (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, `wine64`, 2 runs each): before, executor.process_flood (8 MiB on each of stdout and stderr through `output()`) did not finish within 60 s, and executor.process_interactive_single_worker saw a 20 ms timer on a current-thread runtime fire after 566 to 756 ms while a child that prints nothing for 300 ms was read; after, the flood finishes in 494 to 537 ms, the timer fires after 21 ms, and the 8 process checks pass. Unix pipes are unchanged (they stay on the reactor). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-executor` passes for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-pc-windows-gnu.
- fix(executor): a blocking lookup or connect thread hands its answer over through an `AtomicBox` the waiting future takes, instead of a `OnceLock` the future reads only once it holds the last `Arc` (2026-11-14, Windows runtime probe under Wine 9.0). Before, `on_thread` in crates/core/executor/src/net.rs set the answer, woke the future, and only then dropped its clone of the `Arc` when its closure returned, so a future polled in that window found the answer set but `Arc::into_inner` refused and it returned "a finished thread holds its answer". `lookup_host` takes this path on every platform and Windows' `TcpStream::connect` takes it for every connection. Measured with output/windows-runtime (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, `wine64`): before, one full run failed executor.tcp_single_worker, executor.tcp_refused and executor.lookup_host with that error (`TcpStream::connect` to a closed port returned it after 498 µs instead of ConnectionRefused); after, 4 runs of the 10 timer, TCP and lookup checks and 2 full runs passed them all. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-executor` passes for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-pc-windows-gnu.
- deps(psh): psh-utils compresses with nanocode-compression's miniz and takes its CRC-32 and Adler-32, and its own 1,141-line deflate.rs goes (2026-11-14, cutting vendored code: two miniz_oxide ports lived side by side, psh-utils' in crates/patches/psh and nanocode's in crates/core/compression). What: `codec::compress` (gzip, zip, tar's gzip and git's loose objects) calls the new `nanocode_compression::miniz::compress_to_vec`, `codec::Format` is `miniz::Format`, `codec::crc32` is `checksum::crc32(0, ..)` and `codec::adler32` is `checksum::adler32`; psh-utils keeps its own inflate. `compress_to_vec` is miniz_oxide's `compress_to_vec` loop over nanocode's compressor: output space starts at half the input (at least 2 bytes) and doubles when fewer than 30 bytes are left after a call. Why it is a new function: `miniz::compress` writes through `Writer` in 32 KiB calls, and level 1's fast parser caps a match at the lookahead it has loaded when a call returns, so with different output space the two cut matches at different places: the first harness run with `miniz::compress` differed in 36 of 40,000 cases, all level 1 inputs of 189 to 300 KB whose first differing byte was past 34 KB of output. `miniz::compress` and its callers (PNG, HTTP, nanocode-sim) are unchanged. Equal: output/psh-codec-equal (its own workspace: master's codec.rs, deflate.rs and inflate.rs copied beside this change's codec.rs, with the old codec's `Format` aliased to the new one so both share one inflate) on xorshift-seeded inputs of 0 to 300,000 bytes (literal runs over random alphabets of 1 to 256 symbols mixed with back-references up to 40,000 bytes), random level 1 to 9, random gzip name and mtime: CRC-32, Adler-32 from 1 and from a random start, raw deflate, `compress` raw and zlib, the whole gzip member, both inflate round trips and gunzip agree for seeds 1 to 40 by 5,000 cases, 200,000 cases and 2,000,320 checks with 0 differences, and levels 0, 10, 11 and 255 panic in both. psh-utils' 459 passing tests pass before and after; the same 3 fail before and after because their corpora (awk vendored suites, jq upstream suites, the GNU grep corpus) are not in the tree. Size: the release `nanocode` (x86_64 Linux, stripped) 73,858,184 to 73,833,992 bytes, .text 49,797,112 to 49,784,104; psh-utils' release unit 69.4 to 65.2 s (one run each, `cargo build --release -p nanocode-cli --timings`, CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2, before on a cold build and after rebuilding psh-utils alone). Lines: −1,224, +46. Packages: unchanged (128); psh-utils gains the path dependency nanocode-compression, which the psh workspace's lock adds. Commands: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` (only the warnings master has: rustpython-ruff_python_ast's seven, its cfg warnings and two unused workspace dependencies); `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p nanocode-compression -p nanocode-shell`; in crates/patches/psh `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` and `cargo check --locked -p psh-wasm -p psh-wasm-core --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression --all-targets` (only nanocode-sys's three) and in crates/patches/psh `cargo clippy --locked -p psh-utils --all-targets` (two warnings where master has three; the CRC-32 `chunks_exact` one goes with its table); nanocode-compression is simulated, so `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-sim` and `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 300 2`: passed 300, failed 0, 0 panics. Upstream delta: psh Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, psh-utils Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, src/codec.rs, src/git/store.rs, src/deflate.rs deleted.
- perf(turnlog): `TurnLog::open` sets the writer's `state` to the plain length of the last snapshot row instead of 0 (2026-11-14). `state` is the measured size of the fold that the boundary rule (`hot_bytes > state`) compares against, and `Lease::commit` sets it to the plain length of the snapshot it writes, which is the length that row decodes to. With 0 after a restart, the first commit with any hot event encoded the whole fold with `Fold::snapshot` only to learn that size. In the 10,000-child durable-cloudflare parent restarted from its hill-climb snapshot (one snapshot of 128 MB plain, then 9 rows), that is one full encode before the first model call: `Fold::snapshot` under `Lease::commit` was 10.2% of the profiled wasm restart, with deflate at 1.5%. A reopened writer now holds the value that an uninterrupted writer holds after that snapshot. The rule still measures again once `hot_bytes` passes it, and a log without a snapshot row keeps 0. output/restartcheck (a `MemoryLog` with the 5,414 rows of that parent, `snapshot_rows(Some(64))` as nanocode-ts sets it, then three commits of one event each), 5 interleaved rounds against 5429f51a6: the first commit after open fell from 398-536 ms to 0.1-0.2 ms, `open` took 719-1,065 ms against 637-947 ms on a loaded host, and rows, snapshots and boundaries were identical; on top of the memory lane's streaming `measured` the same commit fell from 112.5-115.7 ms to 0.1 ms. Wasm (durable-cloudflare output/snap-prof.mjs with SNAP_LOAD of that snapshot, `--scenario turn --agents 10000`, nanocode-ts 177b460 on nanocode 22f8297d9 with the OneLog::journals change of 2ccfcecdb, without and with this change; a shared host where the bench lock allowed one clean run of the change): restart to the first model call 4,700, 4,217 and 4,550 ms against 3,874 ms, `sdk.open` 1,321, 1,129 and 1,261 ms against 738 ms, and peak wasm memory 957 MB against 738 MB, because that base built the whole snapshot string to measure it. The crash gate (`scripts/hillclimb.mjs --agents 2000 --scenarios spawn,turn,done,twice` on that bundle) passes with 0 lost and 0 repeated children in every scenario. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-turnlog -- -D warnings`, `cargo +1.97.1 check --locked -p nanocode-turnlog --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; nanocode-sim turns/turnlog sweeps give the same counts with and without this change on 2ccfcecdb plus the memory lane's turnlog commits (`--twice` 0..2000 1669 of 2000, `--snapshot-rows 4 --state-bytes 131072`, `--calm --row-limit 1024` and `--snapshot-ratio 1` 830 of 1000 each, `--long 100` 165 of 200, `--mutation seal_skipped --without restart` caught in 121 of 200), with 0 panics. Every failure is the `cell_rows` check, which fails the same seeds on 2ccfcecdb and 9640273ef without this change.

- A listing open of the JSONL session store reads its directory once (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: every POST.md row ahead of fx). `Sessions::open` ran `clear_temporaries`, a full `read_dir` of `sessions/`, on every open, and listing then read the same directory again in `files`; with 14,600 sessions (29,203 entries) one pass costs 6.5 ms of kernel time (a C `readdir` loop, best of 30), about 63M kernel instructions. `JsonlStore::open_home_in_background`, the CLI's open, whose caller already learns an open failure only from its first operation, now leaves abandoned temporaries to the first job: `list_states` and `list_summaries` clear the dead-pid `.compact-`, `.migrate-` and `.listed-` files they meet in their own scan, every other job runs the standalone pass before its action, and a store that ran no job clears when its worker stops, so an error reaches `close`. A failed pass keeps the `cannot open the session store in <home>` text and is retried by every later job, which all fail until it succeeds, as they did after a failed open; `open`, `open_home` and `open_home_async` still clear while opening. With `ab.py` on BOLT builds (base 5429f51a6, 5 vCPU), `sessions --home` medians over 40 alternating rounds went from 69.8 to 56.7 ms wall, 220.6M to 158.1M instructions:k, 536.2M to 522.9M instructions:u and 118.4 to 107.4 ms task-clock (30 rounds: 66.9 to 58.2 ms); `exec --continue`, which lists, went from 111.6 to 105.4 ms and 233.6M to 170.5M instructions:k over 20 rounds. `sessions <id>` and a fresh `exec`, which never list, still make one pass and are unchanged (74.2M against 74.0M and 74.19M against 74.23M instructions:k, wall within each other's quartiles). An `opendir`-logging LD_PRELOAD shim counted scans of `sessions/`: listing 2 to 1, `exec --continue` 2 to 1, load and fresh `exec` 1 and 1; with `<key>.jsonl.compact-999999-*`, `<key>.jsonl.migrate-999999-*` and `.listed-999999-*` fixtures in a copy of the store, both builds removed them in all four commands and kept live-pid and malformed ones. `sessions --limit 100000`, with and without `--all`, printed the same 14,600 lines from both builds. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-jsonl`, natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy` on it passed with no new warnings.
- `list_summaries` decodes the listed raw summaries on scoped threads, with `recovered`'s policy for the worker count (`cores().min(bytes / JOURNAL_READ_BUFFER_BYTES)`, so a small home decodes inline), after matching the directory to the cache sequentially as before (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track); the decode was about 20% of listing cycles and ran after both scan threads had joined. Measured together (2026-11-14) on the hosted Hand (5 vCPU), each side built by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, BOLT 21) at master f31323105 with and without the five session-listing commits of this date (cached-key sort, raw summaries, overlapped refresh, temporaries without searchers, parallel decode), over a 14,600-session store from bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=store`, alternating runs: `nanocode sessions --home` (30 rounds) wall 113.6 to 76.2 ms (-33%), user instructions 467.2M to 534.3M, kernel 220.1M to 220.9M, page faults 16,895 to 16,792, task clock 117.2 to 117.7 ms, peak RSS 51.8 to 48.9 MB; `nanocode exec --continue` against bench/cli's fake LLM (20 rounds) wall 141.8 to 95.8 ms (-32%), user 545.8M to 612.9M, page faults 18,403 to 18,070, peak RSS 53.9 to 50.5 MB. `sessions --limit 100000` prints the same 14,600 rows with either build, as do a legacy `.summaries.json` home, a cache entry of the wrong type and a store another process resumed into. `cargo check --locked --lib` of the touched crates passes natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown.
